papers.title: An Artificial Immune System-Integrated Redox-Capacitive Biosensing Architecture for Dengue NS1 Detection: A Computational Proof of Concept
papers.abstract: Dengue virus infection remains a major global public health concern, demanding rapid and reliable diagnostic tools. This work introduces a computational proof of concept for an intelligent bioanalytical architecture combining a redox-capacitive biosensing platform with an Artificial Immune System (AIS) machine learning framework to detect the Dengue NS1 protein. Using a simulated dataset of 32 independent sample profiles across 49 frequency points, the AIS algorithm was systematically evaluated on isolated real (C′) and imaginary (C′′) capacitance components under distinct operational scenarios. Utilizing real capacitance (C′), the AIS algorithm achieved 100.0% accuracy in discriminating positive NS1 profiles from controls and negative matrices, while dynamically adapting its Shape Affinity Limen parameter to maintain noise-resilience (83.3% accuracy) in the ambiguous Blank vs. Statistical overlap analysis using the Bhattacharyya Index revealed that imaginary capacitance (C′′) acts as a highly specific complementary marker. While C′′ showed near-total structural overlap (0.995) between blank controls and negative samples—proving physical blindness to background matrix noise—it achieved flawless target identification (100.0% accuracy) for NS1 interaction. Backed by sub-millisecond algorithmic execution times, this dual-channel capacitive–computational framework provides a robust foundation for prospective real-time, point-of-care diagnostic tools.

analysis.summary_en: This study aimed to describe the knowledge, attitude, and practice of preventive medicine students at Hai Phong University of Medicine and Pharmacy regarding the Dengue vaccine and associated factors in 2026. A cross-sectional survey was conducted from December 2025 to May 2026, involving 266 students using a fully randomized online questionnaire. The results showed that 42.5% had adequate knowledge, 39.9% had a positive attitude, and 67.7% had good practice. Regression analysis identified several factors associated with achieving adequate knowledge, including positive attitude, self-study information sources, non-religious beliefs, good practice, and financial capability. The findings highlight the need for targeted educational interventions to improve awareness and behavior among students. However, the study's descriptive nature limits its ability to establish causal relationships, and the evidence is moderate due to the absence of longitudinal or comparative data.

papers.title: Impacto epidemiológico del dengue y del chikungunya en zonas urbanas: revisión sistemática Epidemiological impact of dengue and chikungunya in urban areas: a systematic review
papers.abstract: Objetivo: sintetizar la evidencia sobre el impacto epidemiológico urbano del dengue y del chikungunya. Método: revisión sistemática con síntesis narrativa en PubMed y SciELO (2012-2025); se incluyeron 15 estudios. Resultados: la incidencia mundial del dengue aumentó desde 1990, con diferencias regionales marcadas y alta carga en América Latina. El chikungunya se expandió por las Américas desde 2013 y produjo brotes urbanos explosivos, con manifestaciones articulares persistentes. La urbanización, la expansión de Aedes aegypti y Aedes albopictus y la resistencia a insecticidas favorecieron la transmisión. Destacan como estrategias las nuevas vacunas y el control vectorial integrado. Conclusión: ambas arbovirosis son una carga creciente para las ciudades tropicales y subtropicales y exigen vigilancia y control sostenidos.

analysis.summary_en: This systematic review synthesizes the epidemiological impact of dengue and chikungunya in urban areas. The review, conducted between 2012 and 2025, included 15 studies from PubMed and SciELO. Key findings indicate a global increase in dengue incidence since 1990, with significant regional variations and a high burden in Latin America. Chikungunya expanded across the Americas starting in 2013, causing explosive urban outbreaks with persistent joint manifestations. Urbanization, the spread of Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus, and insecticide resistance are identified as factors that facilitated transmission. The review highlights the need for sustained surveillance and control measures, emphasizing the potential of new vaccines and integrated vector control as strategies. The evidence suggests that both arboviruses pose a growing threat to tropical and subtropical urban populations.

elements_zh.consensus_and_key_conclusions: 结果:1990 年世界登革热事件,拉丁美洲地区市场和货运方面存在差异。基孔肯雅热在 2013 年美洲地区得到扩展,并产生了城市爆炸性的产品,并具有持久的关节表现。

elements_zh.research_and_practice_implications: 强调了新疫苗和综合媒介控制策略的重要性。

papers.title: Estrategias de prevención del dengue en comunidades urbanas: revisión sistemática Dengue prevention strategies in urban communities: a systematic review
papers.abstract: Objetivo: sintetizar la evidencia sobre la efectividad de las estrategias de prevención del dengue en comunidades urbanas y su aplicabilidad al contexto ecuatoriano. Método: revisión sistemática con síntesis narrativa en PubMed y SciELO (2012-2025); se incluyeron 15 estudios: revisiones sistemáticas con y sin metaanálisis, estudios en Ecuador, intervenciones comunitarias y una evaluación económica. Resultados: el control químico aislado redujo los índices entomológicos sin efecto demostrado sobre la transmisión. El manejo ambiental con participación comunitaria, las mallas en las viviendas y las cubiertas de recipientes mostraron los resultados más favorables. El almacenamiento de agua, la percepción del riesgo y la falta de servicios básicos condicionaron la prevención en Ecuador. Conclusión: la prevención del dengue urbano requiere estrategias integradas, comunitarias y sostenidas, con vigilancia epidemiológica y mejoras de los servicios básicos.

analysis.scope_and_question: The review aims to synthesize evidence on the effectiveness of dengue prevention strategies in urban communities and assess their applicability to the Ecuadorian context.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: A systematic review was conducted using PubMed and SciELO databases from 2012 to 2025. The evidence includes 15 studies: systematic reviews with and without meta-analyses, studies conducted in Ecuador, community interventions, and an economic evaluation.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: The review found that integrated, community-based, and sustained strategies, including environmental management, window screens, and covered water containers, showed the most favorable results in dengue prevention. However, chemical control alone reduced entomological indices without demonstrated impact on transmission.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: The review highlights that factors such as water storage practices, risk perception, and lack of basic services influenced prevention effectiveness in Ecuador. There is no explicit mention of conflicting findings or heterogeneity in the results.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: The review concludes that dengue prevention in urban areas requires integrated, community-based, and sustained strategies, along with epidemiological surveillance and improvements in basic services.

analysis.summary_en: This systematic review evaluates dengue prevention strategies in urban communities, focusing on their effectiveness and applicability in Ecuador. The evidence base includes 15 studies from PubMed and SciELO, spanning 2012 to 2025, encompassing systematic reviews, community interventions, and economic evaluations. Key findings indicate that integrated, community-based, and sustained strategies, such as environmental management, window screens, and covered water containers, yielded the most favorable outcomes. However, chemical control alone reduced entomological indices without clear evidence of impact on transmission. The review emphasizes the need for strategies that incorporate epidemiological surveillance and improvements in basic services to effectively prevent dengue in urban settings. The study also notes that factors like water storage practices, risk perception, and lack of basic services influenced prevention success in Ecuador. The implications suggest a focus on community engagement and long-term, sustainable interventions to address dengue in urban populations.

papers.title: Đặc điểm lâm sàng, cận lâm sàng và kết quả điều trị sốc sốt xuất huyết Dengue ở trẻ vị thành niên tại Bệnh viện Đa khoa Tiền Giang Clinical and Paraclinical Characteristics and Treatment Outcomes of Dengue Shock in Adolescents at Tien Giang General Hospital
papers.abstract: Nghiên cứu nhằm mô tả đặc điểm lâm sàng, cận lâm sàng và kết quả điều trị sốc sốt xuất huyết Dengue(SXHD) ở trẻ vị thành niên (từ 13 đến dưới 16 tuổi) tại Bệnh viện Đa khoa Tiền Giang. Nghiên cứu cắtngang có phân tích, hồi cứu hồ sơ bệnh án của 35 trẻ được chẩn đoán sốc SXHD trong giai đoạn 7/2023–7/2025. Tuổi trung bình là 14,5 ± 0,9 tuổi; nam chiếm 48,6%. 51,4% trẻ thừa cân hoặc béo phì và 22,9% cósốc SXHD nặng. Phần lớn trẻ vào sốc ở ngày bệnh thứ 5–6 (62,9%). Khi vào sốc, hematocrit trung bình là49,4 ± 4,8%, tiểu cầu 32.549 ± 16.167 tế bào/mm3; 77,1% có lactate ≥ 2 mmol/L và 28,6% có AST và/hoặcALT ≥ 400 U/L. Dung dịch cao phân tử được sử dụng ở 77,1% trường hợp; tổng lượng dịch truyền trungbình là 148,2 ± 41,6 mL/kg. Nghiên cứu cắtngang có phân tích, hồi cứu hồ sơ bệnh án của 35 trẻ được chẩn đoán sốc SXHD trong giai đoạn 7/2023–7/2025. Khi vào sốc, hematocrit trung bình là49,4 ± 4,8%, tiểu cầu 32.549 ± 16.167 tế bào/mm3; 77,1% có lactate ≥ 2 mmol/L và 28,6% có AST và/hoặcALT ≥ 400 U/L. news.title_original: WHO Health Emergencies EPI-WIN webinar: Launch of WHO guidelines for clinical management of arboviral diseases: dengue, chikungunya, Zika and yellow fever - World Health Organization (WHO)

analysis.time: The webinar was launched on 2 November 2026, with related activities occurring from 4 November 2026 to 13 November 2026.
analysis.location_and_population: The event was hosted by the World Health Organization (WHO) globally, with a specific mention of Sudan's polio vaccination campaign involving around 11 million children.
analysis.event: WHO launched guidelines for the clinical management of arboviral diseases, including dengue, chikungunya, Zika, and yellow fever, through a webinar. This was part of a broader set of activities related to health emergencies and disease outbreaks.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The guidelines aim to improve clinical management and response to arboviral diseases, which are significant public health threats. The WHO also highlighted ongoing efforts in polio vaccination campaigns and other health initiatives.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The guidelines were launched as part of WHO's ongoing efforts to address health emergencies. The polio vaccination campaign in Sudan was reported as a nationwide initiative with support from multiple partners.

analysis.brief_en: The World Health Organization (WHO) launched guidelines for the clinical management of arboviral diseases, including dengue, chikungunya, Zika, and yellow fever, through a webinar on 2 November 2026. These guidelines are part of WHO's broader efforts to address health emergencies and improve disease response. The event was accompanied by other activities, such as a polio vaccination campaign in Sudan involving around 11 million children, which was conducted from October to November 2026 with support from WHO, UNICEF, and other partners. Additionally, WHO highlighted ongoing initiatives related to health emergencies, including the launch of a global mega-map and other reports on disease outbreaks and health-related challenges. The guidelines aim to enhance clinical management and preparedness for arboviral diseases, which pose significant public health risks worldwide.

news.title_zh: 世界卫生组织(WHO)健康紧急事件EPI-WIN网络研讨会:发布登革热、基孔肯雅热、寨卡病毒和黄热病临床管理指南 - 世界卫生组织(WHO)
news.source_body_en: The World Health Organization (WHO) launched guidelines for the clinical management of arboviral diseases, including dengue, chikungunya, Zika, and yellow fever, through a webinar on 2 November 2026. These guidelines are part of WHO's broader efforts to address health emergencies and improve disease response. The event was accompanied by other activities, such as a polio vaccination campaign in Sudan involving around 11 million children, which was conducted from October to November 2026 with support from WHO, UNICEF, and other partners. Additionally, WHO highlighted ongoing initiatives related to health emergencies, including the launch of a global mega-map and other reports on disease outbreaks and health-related challenges. The guidelines aim to enhance clinical management and preparedness for arboviral diseases, which pose significant public health risks worldwide.
news.content_zh: 世界卫生组织 (WHO) 在 2026 年 11 月 2 日的网络研讨会上发布了登革热、基孔肯雅热、寨卡病毒和黄热病等虫媒病毒性疾病的临床管理指南。这些指南是世卫组织应对突发卫生事件和改善疾病应对的更广泛努力的一部分。该活动还伴随着其他活动,例如在世卫组织、联合国儿童基金会和其他合作伙伴的支持下于 2026 年 10 月至 11 月在苏丹开展的脊髓灰质炎 疫苗接种 运动,涉及约 1100 万儿童。此外,世卫组织还强调了与突发卫生事件有关的持续举措,包括推出全球大型地图以及有关疾病 暴发 和健康相关挑战的其他报告。该指南旨在加强虫媒病毒性疾病的临床管理和防备,虫媒病毒性疾病在全球范围内构成了重大的公共卫生风险。

news.content: Skip to main content Help Log in ReliefWeb Search Content Search What are you looking for? Search|t Updates Countries Disasters Organizations Topics Jobs Training Informing humanitarians worldwide 24/7 — a service provided by UN OCHA World + 15 more Epidemic and emerging disease alerts in the Pacific as of 03 November 2026 Format Map Source SPC Posted 3 Nov 2026 Originally published 3 Nov 2026 Attachments Download Map (PDF | 569.56 KB) Highlights/updates since the last map was sent on PacNet on 27 October 2026: Dengue • American Samoa: The Department of Health Situational Report for 19 to 25 October 2026 records 1,064 laboratory-confirmed dengue cases as of 27 October 2026 since the outbreak began in 2025. New case numbers remain low, with four cases reported over the last three EpiWeeks: two cases in EpiWeek 40 and one case each in EpiWeeks 41 and 42. Dengue cases peaked in early 2026 (EpiWeek 02), with weekly case counts remaining low since May. The blue alert for dengue (DENV-1 & DENV-2) remains in effect. – Source: American Samoa Department of Health, Situational Report: Respiratory & Notifiable Diseases shared with the PPHSN Coordinating Body Focal point on 30 October 2026. • Marshall Islands: The 16th Outbreak Situation Report covering 15 August to 22 October 2026, records 165 positive cases (confirmed and probable) among 540 specimens tested: 127 in Majuro and 38 in Ebeye, compared with 124 and 32 cases, respectively, in the previous report covering 15 August to 15 October 2026. There have been 15 hospitalisations (13 in Majuro and two in Ebeye) and no deaths since the beginning of the outbreak. Attack rates are 5.5 per 1,000 population in Majuro and 3.9 per 1,000 in Ebeye, while positivity rates are 29% and 37%, respectively. Only DENV-1 has been identified. Vector control has been completed at the households of 147 positive cases and at 206 sites. About 250 spatial repellents and mosquito nets have been delivered to Ebeye, and surveillance in the neighbouring islands is being strengthened. The red alert for dengue (DENV-1) remains in effect. – Source: Republic of the Marshall Islands Ministry of Health and Human Services, 16th Outbreak Situation Report on dengue fever in Majuro and Ebeye accessed on 03 November 2026. • Samoa: Dengue Fever Outbreak Situation Report Issue No. 79, covering EpiWeek 42 (12 to 18 October 2026), reports 51 new cases, down 4% on the previous week (53, revised from 14), with no laboratory-confirmed case, no new admission and no death. Since 01 January 2025, 20,478 clinically diagnosed cases, 5,547 laboratory-confirmed cases and nine dengue-related deaths have been recorded. DENV-1 accounts for 52% and DENV-2 for 48% of serotyped cases, and children under 15 years for 73% of cases. The blue alert for dengue (DENV-1 & DENV-2) remains in effect. – Source: Ministry of Health Samoa, Dengue Fever Outbreak Situation Report Issue No. 79 accessed on 03 November 2026. Diarrhea • Federated States of Micronesia – Yap State: The Yap weekly bulletin for EpiWeek 43 (19 to 25 October 2026) shows diarrhoea on alert for a tenth consecutive week, rising from 9 to 15 cases, above the alert threshold of 7. All 5 stool specimens tested on the BioFire gastrointestinal panel were positive: three patients had adenovirus, two of them co-infected with E. coli pathotypes, and two had E. coli pathotype co-infections only. Among 100 diarrhoea cases in children aged 0 to 5 years since the start of the outbreak, 34 had completed rotavirus vaccination, 27 were partially vaccinated, 28 were unvaccinated and 11 had their status still being verified. The blue alert for rotavirus is changed to blue alert for diarrhea for the Federated States of Micronesia (Yap State). – Source: Yap State Department of Health Services, Communicable Disease Weekly Bulletin, shared with the PPHSN Coordinating Body Focal point on 29 October 2026. Measles • Australia: On 30 October 2026, the Western Australia Department of Health confirmed a new measles case in a young child treated at a Perth hospital. The case is not linked to overseas travel and has no known link to the case reported on 28 October, and the Department says that a locally acquired case with no known source raises concern for undetected community transmission. The earlier case is a returned overseas traveller who visited several public venues in Perth while infectious. People who attended the listed exposure locations are advised to monitor for symptoms and to call ahead before visiting a GP clinic or emergency department. As of 03 November 2026 at the national level, 122 measles notifications have been recorded in Australia, compared with 181 in 2025. The red alert for measles remains in effect for Australia. – Sources: Western Australia Department of Health, Measles alert for Perth in returned overseas traveller, Western Australia Department of Health, WA Health confirms new measles case in young child and Dashboard · NINDSS Portal accessed on 03 November 2026. • Papua New Guinea: The National Department of Health weekly bulletin for EpiWeek 43 (19 to 25 October 2026) reports 26 acute fever and rash cases nationally, down from 30 in EpiWeek 42. Year to date, 452 cases have been reported and 396 samples tested, with 19 IgM-positive measles results. After Expert Review Group review, two measles cases (New Ireland 1, Western Highlands 1) and two rubella cases are confirmed in 2026. The last IgM-positive measles onset was on 15 September 2026 and the last rubella onset on 29 September 2026. The measles-rubella vaccination campaign targets all children under seven in districts with a detected case. The red alert for measles remains in effect for Papua New Guinea. – Source: Papua New Guinea National Department of Health, Public Health Events Weekly Bulletin, shared with the PPHSN Coordinating Body Focal point on 30 October 2026. Respiratory diseases • French Polynesia: In French Polynesia, influenza activity increased markedly in EpiWeek 43 (19–25 October 2026), confirming the territory’s entry into an epidemic phase. A total of 52 laboratory-confirmed influenza A cases, predominantly A(H1N1), were reported during the week, with 14 hospitalisations. Increased cases and hospitalisations were observed in Tahiti, Raiatea and the Marquesas, indicating circulation across several parts of the territory. The seasonal influenza vaccination campaign began on 26 October, with vaccination available through pharmacies and health facilities. A red alert for influenza A is issued for French Polynesia. – Source: Agence de régulation de l'action sanitaire et sociale (ARASS), Bulletin de Surveillance Sanitaire de Polynésie française n°38 shared with the PPHSN Coordinating Body Focal point on 03 November 2026. • New Zealand: For the week ending 25 October 2026, the all-cause SARI hospitalisation rate in the Auckland region remained stable and in the low activity band. The influenza-positive SARI hospitalisation rate increased slightly but also remained low. Influenza remained the most commonly detected virus among SARI patients, with 17 positive samples, and SARI influenza test positivity increased from 19.0% to 28.3%. Positivity among sentinel GP influenza-like illness cases also increased, from 9.5% to 13.0%. In 2026 to date, 707 of 2,924 (24.2%) SARI samples and 229 of 1,220 (18.8%) sentinel GP samples have tested positive for influenza. The blue alert for influenza A remains in effect for New Zealand. – Source: New Zealand acute respiratory illness dashboard accessed on 03 November 2026. • Tonga: The weekly syndromic surveillance report for EpiWeek 43 (19 to 25 October 2026) shows influenza-like illness (ILI) falling for a second week, from 125 to 84 cases, after the EpiWeek 41 peak of 137. Severe acute respiratory infection (SARI) fell from 13 to 9 cases. From 03 August to 25 October 2026, 89 SARI patients were hospitalised. Of 732 ILI cases, 499 (68.1%) were tested: 235 (47%) were positive for influenza A, 6 for influenza B and 29 for RSV. Four deaths have occurred among SARI cases, unchanged since EpiWeek 42, three of them laboratory-confirmed influenza A. The red alert for influenza A remains in effect for Tonga. – Source: Tonga Ministry of Health, Weekly Communicable Diseases Syndromic Surveillance shared with the PPHSN Coordinating Body Focal point on 30 October 2026. Rotavirus • Vanuatu: Situation Update No. 1 on watery diarrhoea on Ambae Island, Penama Province covering 12 to 18 October 2026, reports seven cases in the period, below the weekly alert threshold of 8. Two laboratory-confirmed rotavirus cases were detected in EpiWeek 43, both from Navonda village in East Ambae, confirming ongoing transmission. The Ministry of Health states that the current data do not support an outbreak declaration: from week 1 to week 42, weekly counts at Lolowai Hospital exceeded the threshold only once, in week 10. Most cases are aged over 5 years (59%) and 75% come from East Ambae. One case was admitted and discharged, with no severe case and no death. Enhanced surveillance, active case finding, risk communication on hygiene and safe water, and testing of suspected cases are under way. The red alert for rotavirus is changed to blue alert for rotavirus for Vanuatu. – Source: Vanuatu Ministry of Health, Watery Diarrhoea on Ambae Island, Penama Province, Situation Update No. 1, shared with the PPHSN Coordinating Body Focal point on 28 October 2026. Other Information: One Health - High pathogenicity avian influenza • Australia: A dead common dolphin that washed ashore at Encounter Bay on South Australia's Fleurieu Peninsula tested positive for avian influenza (H5), according to the state's chief veterinary officer, who assessed the risk of an extensive outbreak among dolphins as low while flagging ongoing concern for seals and sea lions. South Australia has recorded 341 positive H5 events and Australia 732 confirmed events in wildlife as of 02 November 2026. New detections are less frequent, with no recent mass mortality. Vaccine has been released for wild little penguin colonies at Granite Island, Penneshaw and Emu Bay, with no start date set. H5 has not been reported from any Pacific Island country or territory to date. – Source: BEACON, HPAI detected in a dolphin, South Australia, Australia as federal government rolls out wildlife vaccination and Latest data - DAFF accessed on 03 November 2026. • Hawai’i: On 29 October 2026, the Hawaiʻi State Department of Health reported that genomic sequencing identified H5N1 genetic material, genotype D1.1, in a wastewater sample collected on 14 October 2026 at a site in East Kauaʻi. It is the first detection of this genotype in Hawaiʻi, where genotype A3 was previously found. The detection does not mean that live, infectious virus is or has been present in a human. No human case has been linked to this signal and no H5N1 has been detected in local dairy milk testing. – Source: Hawaiʻi Department of Health, DOH reports H5N1 avian flu detected in Kauaʻi County wastewater sample accessed on 03 November 2026. • Japan: A dead wild goose recovered in Kurihara City, Miyagi Prefecture, on 27 October 2026 tested preliminarily positive for avian influenza virus. The Environment Ministry is awaiting genetic confirmation of whether the strain is of high pathogenicity, which would be the first such detection in a wild bird in Japan this season. A 10 km priority zone for wild bird monitoring has been designated around the site. No poultry, mammal or human case has been reported. – Source: BEACON, First preliminary positive detection of avian influenza in a wild goose this migratory season in Japan accessed on 03 November 2026. Many thanks again for your continuous contributions. Please note that the alerts displayed on the map are based on information available to us as of the date of this report. New case numbers remain low, with four cases reported over the last three EpiWeeks: two cases in EpiWeek 40 and one case each in EpiWeeks 41 and 42. Dengue cases peaked in early 2026 (EpiWeek 02), with weekly case counts remaining low since May. The blue alert for dengue (DENV-1 & DENV-2) remains in effect. – Source: American Samoa Department of Health, Situational Report: Respiratory & Notifiable Diseases shared with the PPHSN Coordinating Body Focal point on 30 October 2026. • Marshall Islands: The 16th Outbreak Situation Report covering 15 August to 22 October 2026, records 165 positive cases (confirmed and probable) among 540 specimens tested: 127 in Majuro and 38 in Ebeye, compared with 124 and 32 cases, respectively, in the previous report covering 15 August to 15 October 2026. There have been 15 hospitalisations (13 in Majuro and two in Ebeye) and no deaths since the beginning of the outbreak. Attack rates are 5.5 per 1,000 population in Majuro and 3.9 per 1,000 in Ebeye, while positivity rates are 29% and 37%, respectively. Only DENV-1 has been identified. Vector control has been completed at the households of 147 positive cases and at 206 sites. About 250 spatial repellents and mosquito nets have been delivered to Ebeye, and surveillance in the neighbouring islands is being strengthened. The red alert for dengue (DENV-1) remains in effect. – Source: Republic of the Marshall Islands Ministry of Health and Human Services, 16th Outbreak Situation Report on dengue fever in Majuro and Ebeye accessed on 03 November 2026. • Samoa: Dengue Fever Outbreak Situation Report Issue No. 79, covering EpiWeek 42 (12 to 18 October 2026), reports 51 new cases, down 4% on the previous week (53, revised from 14), with no laboratory-confirmed case, no new admission and no death. Since 01 January 2025, 20,478 clinically diagnosed cases, 5,547 laboratory-confirmed cases and nine dengue-related deaths have been recorded. DENV-1 accounts for 52% and DENV-2 for 48% of serotyped cases, and children under 15 years for 73% of cases. The blue alert for dengue (DENV-1 & DENV-2) remains in effect. – Source: Ministry of Health Samoa, Dengue Fever Outbreak Situation Report Issue No. 79 accessed on 03 November 2026. Diarrhea • Federated States of Micronesia – Yap State: The Yap weekly bulletin for EpiWeek 43 (19 to 25 October 2026) shows diarrhoea on alert for a tenth consecutive week, rising from 9 to 15 cases, above the alert threshold of 7. All 5 stool specimens tested on the BioFire gastrointestinal panel were positive: three patients had adenovirus, two of them co-infected with E. coli pathotypes, and two had E. coli pathotype co-infections only. Among 100 diarrhoea cases in children aged 0 to 5 years since the start of the outbreak, 34 had completed rotavirus vaccination, 27 were partially vaccinated, 28 were unvaccinated and 11 had their status still being verified. The blue alert for rotavirus is changed to blue alert for diarrhea for the Federated States of Micronesia (Yap State). – Source: Yap State Department of Health Services, Communicable Disease Weekly Bulletin, shared with the PPHSN Coordinating Body Focal point on 29 October 2026. Measles • Australia: On 30 October 2026, the Western Australia Department of Health confirmed a new measles case in a young child treated at a Perth hospital. The case is not linked to overseas travel and has no known link to the case reported on 28 October, and the Department says that a locally acquired case with no known source raises concern for undetected community transmission. The earlier case is a returned overseas traveller who visited several public venues in Perth while infectious. People who attended the listed exposure locations are advised to monitor for symptoms and to call ahead before visiting a GP clinic or emergency department. As of 03 November 2026 at the national level, 122 measles notifications have been recorded in Australia, compared with 181 in 2025. The red alert for measles remains in effect for Australia. – Sources: Western Australia Department of Health, Measles alert for Perth in returned overseas traveller, Western Australia Department of Health, WA Health confirms new measles case in young child and Dashboard · NINDSS Portal accessed on 03 November 2026. • Papua New Guinea: The National Department of Health weekly bulletin for EpiWeek 43 (19 to 25 October 2026) reports 26 acute fever and rash cases nationally, down from 30 in EpiWeek 42. Year to date, 452 cases have been reported and 396 samples tested, with 19 IgM-positive measles results. After Expert Review Group review, two measles cases (New Ireland 1, Western Highlands 1) and two rubella cases are confirmed in 2026. The last IgM-positive measles onset was on 15 September 2026 and the last rubella onset on 29 September 2026. The measles-rubella vaccination campaign targets all children under seven in districts with a detected case. The red alert for measles remains in effect for Papua New Guinea. – Source: Papua New Guinea National Department of Health, Public Health Events Weekly Bulletin, shared with the PPHSN Coordinating Body Focal point on 30 October 2026. Respiratory diseases • French Polynesia: In French Polynesia, influenza activity increased markedly in EpiWeek 43 (19–25 October 2026), confirming the territory’s entry into an epidemic phase. A total of 52 laboratory-confirmed influenza A cases, predominantly A(H1N1), were reported during the week, with 14 hospitalisations. Increased cases and hospitalisations were observed in Tahiti, Raiatea and the Marquesas, indicating circulation across several parts of the territory. The seasonal influenza vaccination campaign began on 26 October, with vaccination available through pharmacies and health facilities. A red alert for influenza A is issued for French Polynesia. – Source: Agence de régulation de l'action sanitaire et sociale (ARASS), Bulletin de Surveillance Sanitaire de Polynésie française n°38 shared with the PPHSN Coordinating Body Focal point on 03 November 2026. • New Zealand: For the week ending 25 October 2026, the all-cause SARI hospitalisation rate in the Auckland region remained stable and in the low activity band. The influenza-positive SARI hospitalisation rate increased slightly but also remained low. Influenza remained the most commonly detected virus among SARI patients, with 17 positive samples, and SARI influenza test positivity increased from 19.0% to 28.3%. Positivity among sentinel GP influenza-like illness cases also increased, from 9.5% to 13.0%. In 2026 to date, 707 of 2,924 (24.2%) SARI samples and 229 of 1,220 (18.8%) sentinel GP samples have tested positive for influenza. The blue alert for influenza A remains in effect for New Zealand. – Source: New Zealand acute respiratory illness dashboard accessed on 03 November 2026. • Tonga: The weekly syndromic surveillance report for EpiWeek 43 (19 to 25 October 2026) shows influenza-like illness (ILI) falling for a second week, from 125 to 84 cases, after the EpiWeek 41 peak of 137. Severe acute respiratory infection (SARI) fell from 13 to 9 cases. From 03 August to 25 October 2026, 89 SARI patients were hospitalised. Of 732 ILI cases, 499 (68.1%) were tested: 235 (47%) were positive for influenza A, 6 for influenza B and 29 for RSV. Four deaths have occurred among SARI cases, unchanged since EpiWeek 42, three of them laboratory-confirmed influenza A. The red alert for influenza A remains in effect for Tonga. – Source: Tonga Ministry of Health, Weekly Communicable Diseases Syndromic Surveillance shared with the PPHSN Coordinating Body Focal point on 30 October 2026. Rotavirus • Vanuatu: Situation Update No. 1 on watery diarrhoea on Ambae Island, Penama Province covering 12 to 18 October 2026, reports seven cases in the period, below the weekly alert threshold of 8. Two laboratory-confirmed rotavirus cases were detected in EpiWeek 43, both from Navonda village in East Ambae, confirming ongoing transmission. The Ministry of Health states that the current data do not support an outbreak declaration: from week 1 to week 42, weekly counts at Lolowai Hospital exceeded the threshold only once, in week 10. Most cases are aged over 5 years (59%) and 75% come from East Ambae. One case was admitted and discharged, with no severe case and no death. Enhanced surveillance, active case finding, risk communication on hygiene and safe water, and testing of suspected cases are under way. The red alert for rotavirus is changed to blue alert for rotavirus for Vanuatu. – Source: Vanuatu Ministry of Health, Watery Diarrhoea on Ambae Island, Penama Province, Situation Update No. 1, shared with the PPHSN Coordinating Body Focal point on 28 October 2026. No human case has been linked to this signal and no H5N1 has been detected in local dairy milk testing. – Source: Hawaiʻi Department of Health, DOH reports H5N1 avian flu detected in Kauaʻi County wastewater sample accessed on 03 November 2026. • Japan: A dead wild goose recovered in Kurihara City, Miyagi Prefecture, on 27 October 2026 tested preliminarily positive for avian influenza virus. The Environment Ministry is awaiting genetic confirmation of whether the strain is of high pathogenicity, which would be the first such detection in a wild bird in Japan this season. A 10 km priority zone for wild bird monitoring has been designated around the site. No poultry, mammal or human case has been reported. – Source: BEACON, First preliminary positive detection of avian influenza in a wild goose this migratory season in Japan accessed on 03 November 2026. news.content: 12:44 AM Thursday, 5th November UrduMatrimonialsClassifieds مزید دریافت کریں صحافتی آرٹیکلز اٹلس نقشے دیکھیں مقامی گائیڈ دیکھیں مزید دریافت کریں آن لائن خبریں اخبار کی فراہمی تازہ ترین خبریں الیکٹرانک پیپر نیوز الرٹس World Business Sports Entertainment Health Crime Edu and Jobs Politics Photos Videos Menu Home > Health India's first dengue vaccine due in 2027: Japanese pharma Wed 04 Nov 2026, 23:52:56 India’s first dengue vaccine, Japanese pharma major Takeda’s Qdenga, is expected to reach the private market in the first half of 2027, offering a new tool against a disease that infects millions worldwide and causes recurring outbreaks across the country. Clinicians, however, urge caution. Some of them cite unanswered questions about protection against different strains, how long immunity lasts and the risk of severe disease in later infections. The Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO) authorised Qdenga in July for people aged four to 60. Takeda will launch it in India with Dr Reddy’s Laboratories. Until now, no widely available vaccine existed for protection against dengue – the world’s fastest-growing mosquito-borne disease. A World Health ORGnisation surveillance system recorded 14.1 million cases worldwide in 2024, the highest ever reported, and cases appeared in more than 100 countries. India is part of that picture. Here, reported cases rose from 44,585 in 2020 to 1,93,245 in 2021, and 2024 saw 233,519 cases and 297 deaths. Cases fell to 1,13,440 and 94 deaths through November 2025, the lowest since 2021, but official counts understate the real burden. One Indian study estimated actual cases at 282 times the number reported, and dengue is now a year-round problem rather than a seasonal one. Against this background, the promise of a vaccine offers hope. But some clinicians insist that the evidence on the vaccine needs closer scrutiny before wide adoption. Leading paediatrician Dr Sanjeev Bagai shared his concerns, which include the virus’s evolution, differences in circulating strains across India and antibody-dependent enhancement (ADE), in which the immune response from an earlier infection can make a later one more severe. Dr Bagai’s first concern is durability. Trial results are encouraging: Qdenga protected against virologically confirmed dengue and reduced dengue-related hospitalisations, though protection varies by serotype and by whether a person had been exposed before. A longer-term analysis of the pivotal trial, published by the manufacturer, reported efficacy of 61.2% against confirmed dengue and 84.1% against hospitalisation 4.5 years after vaccination. That is meaningful protection, but it does not stop every infection. Dr Bagai wants closer scrutiny of how protection changes in later years, especially for individual serotypes. “The problem is that people look at the مزید دریافت کریں بریکنگ نیوز ای پیپر سبسکرپشن ای بکس تلاش کریں top-line vaccine efficacy figures without examining what happens to protection over three or four years,” he says. He also questions whether trial data adequately represent India’s diverse population and the geography of dengue. Waning protection, however, is not evidence of harm. A decline in efficacy does not by itself show that later infections become more severe. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends Qdenga for children aged six to 16 in high-transmission settings but flags uncertainty about protection against DENV-3 and DENV-4 in people never previously infected. It advises against routine introduction in low-to-moderate transmission areas until more evidence emerges, and urges countries to account for regional differences in transmission rather than adopt a uniform strategy. Dr Bagai’s most serious concern is ADE. Antibodies from an earlier infection may fail to neutralise a later one and can help the virus enter cells, raising the risk of severe disease. Dengue is among the best-known examples: a second infection with a different serotype can trigger a stronger inflammatory response and complications. Because people’s exposure histories differ widely,Dr Bagai says vaccinations must be examined in this light. “If you are giving a vaccine, you need to understand how the body’s existing immune status is going to respond to it,” he says. He also suggests that prior infections such as COVID-19 and influenza could shape responses to dengue vaccination through similarities in immune-recognition pathways. But claims that shared protein sequences could make the body respond as if facing another dengue infection are not established clinical evidence of ADE after Qdenga. They would need specific validation. Dr Sumit Jain, director of internal medicine at Paras Health, Panchkula, agrees that ADE has historically worried dengue vaccination but says the risk cannot be assumed for every vaccine. “Dengvaxia’s experience shouldn’t be assumed to be representative of the risk profile of any new dengue vaccine,” he says. Sanofi’s Dengvaxia has a different formulation and is restricted to people with evidence of prior infection, because those never infected face a higher risk of severe dengue after vaccination and later exposure. Qdenga has been through separate trials and is approved in India without proof of previous infection. That does not settle every safety question. Its risk profile must be judged on its own clinical and post-marketing evidence. مزید دریافت کریں ٹریول گائیڈ پڑھیں آن لائن میگزین دیسی ملبوسات Share Tweet No Comments For This Post, Be first to write a Comment. news.content_original: 12:44 AM Thursday, 5th November UrduMatrimonialsClassifieds مزید دریافت کریں صحافتی آرٹیکلز اٹلس نقشے دیکھیں مقامی گائیڈ دیکھیں مزید دریافت کریں آن لائن خبریں اخبار کی فراہمی تازہ ترین خبریں الیکٹرانک پیپر نیوز الرٹس World Business Sports Entertainment Health Crime Edu and Jobs Politics Photos Videos Menu Home > Health India's first dengue vaccine due in 2027: Japanese pharma Wed 04 Nov 2026, 23:52:56 India’s first dengue vaccine, Japanese pharma major Takeda’s Qdenga, is expected to reach the private market in the first half of 2027, offering a new tool against a disease that infects millions worldwide and causes recurring outbreaks across the country. Clinicians, however, urge caution. Some of them cite unanswered questions about protection against different strains, how long immunity lasts and the risk of severe disease in later infections. The Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO) authorised Qdenga in July for people aged four to 60. Takeda will launch it in India with Dr Reddy’s Laboratories. Until now, no widely available vaccine existed for protection against dengue – the world’s fastest-growing mosquito-borne disease. A World Health ORGnisation surveillance system recorded 14.1 million cases worldwide in 2024, the highest ever reported, and cases appeared in more than 100 countries. India is part of that picture. Here, reported cases rose from 44,585 in 2020 to 1,93,245 in 2021, and 2024 saw 233,519 cases and 297 deaths. Cases fell to 1,13,440 and 94 deaths through November 2025, the lowest since 2021, but official counts understate the real burden. One Indian study estimated actual cases at 282 times the number reported, and dengue is now a year-round problem rather than a seasonal one. Against this background, the promise of a vaccine offers hope. But some clinicians insist that the evidence on the vaccine needs closer scrutiny before wide adoption. Leading paediatrician Dr Sanjeev Bagai shared his concerns, which include the virus’s evolution, differences in circulating strains across India and antibody-dependent enhancement (ADE), in which the immune response from an earlier infection can make a later one more severe. Dr Bagai’s first concern is durability. Trial results are encouraging: Qdenga protected against virologically confirmed dengue and reduced dengue-related hospitalisations, though protection varies by serotype and by whether a person had been exposed before. A longer-term analysis of the pivotal trial, published by the manufacturer, reported efficacy of 61.2% against confirmed dengue and 84.1% against hospitalisation 4.5 years after vaccination. That is meaningful protection, but it does not stop every infection. Dr Bagai wants closer scrutiny of how protection changes in later years, especially for individual serotypes. “The problem is that people look at the مزید دریافت کریں بریکنگ نیوز ای پیپر سبسکرپشن ای بکس تلاش کریں top-line vaccine efficacy figures without examining what happens to protection over three or four years,” he says. He also questions whether trial data adequately represent India’s diverse population and the geography of dengue. Waning protection, however, is not evidence of harm. A decline in efficacy does not by itself show that later infections become more severe. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends Qdenga for children aged six to 16 in high-transmission settings but flags uncertainty about protection against DENV-3 and DENV-4 in people never previously infected. It advises against routine introduction in low-to-moderate transmission areas until more evidence emerges, and urges countries to account for regional differences in transmission rather than adopt a uniform strategy. Dr Bagai’s most serious concern is ADE. Antibodies from an earlier infection may fail to neutralise a later one and can help the virus enter cells, raising the risk of severe disease. Dengue is among the best-known examples: a second infection with a different serotype can trigger a stronger inflammatory response and complications. Because people’s exposure histories differ widely,Dr Bagai says vaccinations must be examined in this light. “If you are giving a vaccine, you need to understand how the body’s existing immune status is going to respond to it,” he says. He also suggests that prior infections such as COVID-19 and influenza could shape responses to dengue vaccination through similarities in immune-recognition pathways. But claims that shared protein sequences could make the body respond as if facing another dengue infection are not established clinical evidence of ADE after Qdenga. They would need specific validation. Dr Sumit Jain, director of internal medicine at Paras Health, Panchkula, agrees that ADE has historically worried dengue vaccination but says the risk cannot be assumed for every vaccine. “Dengvaxia’s experience shouldn’t be assumed to be representative of the risk profile of any new dengue vaccine,” he says. Sanofi’s Dengvaxia has a different formulation and is restricted to people with evidence of prior infection, because those never infected face a higher risk of severe dengue after vaccination and later exposure. Qdenga has been through separate trials and is approved in India without proof of previous infection. That does not settle every safety question. Its risk profile must be judged on its own clinical and post-marketing evidence. مزید دریافت کریں ٹریول گائیڈ پڑھیں آن لائن میگزین دیسی ملبوسات Share Tweet No Comments For This Post, Be first to write a Comment. An initial infection may be mild or unnoticed, but subsequent infection with a different serotype increases the risk of severe illness in some cases. Sweta Mitra November 04, 2026 - 11:46 AM Join Follow Follow Dengue Vaccine: The Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO) approved Qdenga in July for individuals aged four to 60. Takeda plans to launch the vaccine in India in partnership with Dr Reddy’s Laboratories. Until now, there has been no widely accessible vaccine to protect against dengue, which is the fastest-growing mosquito-borne disease globally. According to a World Health Organisation surveillance system, 14.1 million cases were recorded worldwide in 2024, the highest number ever documented, with cases reported in over 100 countries. India is included in this global situation. Dengue Vaccine Update In India, reported dengue cases increased from 44,585 in 2020 to 193,245 in 2021, with 233,519 cases and 297 deaths recorded in 2024. By November 2025, cases had dropped to 113,440 with 94 deaths, the lowest figures since 2021, though official statistics underestimate the true scale of the problem. One Indian study estimated that actual cases could be 282 times higher than reported, and dengue has become a year-round issue rather than one confined to certain seasons. Against this backdrop, the introduction of a vaccine offers hope. However, some clinicians argue that the evidence supporting the vaccine requires more thorough evaluation before it is widely adopted. Prominent paediatrician Dr Sanjeev Bagai has expressed concerns, including the virus’s evolution, regional variations in circulating strains across India, and antibody-dependent enhancement (ADE), where the immune response from a prior infection may worsen a subsequent one. Dengue is primarily transmitted through the bite of infected Aedes aegypti mosquitoes and has four serotypes, DENV-1 to DENV-4. Infection with one serotype does not confer immunity against the others, meaning individuals can be infected multiple times. An initial infection may be mild or unnoticed, but subsequent infection with a different serotype increases the risk of severe illness in some cases. This presents a major challenge for vaccine development. India’s dengue burden is further complicated by several serotypes circulating in different regions. Dr Bagai notes that dominant strains vary geographically and shift over time. “It is impossible to predict which strain will dominate in which region of India at any given time of year,” he explains. He also highlights coinfections involving multiple serotypes and genetic changes in the virus, which complicate assessments of a vaccine’s nationwide effectiveness. Qdenga is a tetravalent vaccine designed to target all four serotypes, but it is developed using a weakened DENV-2 backbone into which the genes for the surface proteins of the other serotypes are inserted. Dr Bagai questions whether this approach ensures balanced protection given the variability in circulating strains. Nonetheless, the vaccine does include components for all four serotypes and is not solely targeted at DENV-2. Dr Bagai’s initial concern relates to the duration of protection. Trial results are promising: Qdenga has been shown to protect against virologically confirmed dengue and reduce dengue-related hospitalisations, although efficacy varies by serotype and prior exposure. A long-term analysis of the pivotal trial, published by the manufacturer, reported an efficacy of 61.2% against confirmed dengue and 84.1% against hospitalisation 4.5 years post-vaccination. While this represents significant protection, it does not prevent all infections. Dr Bagai calls for closer examination of how protection evolves over subsequent years, particularly for individual serotypes. What is the issue? “The issue is that people tend to focus on headline vaccine efficacy numbers without considering how protection changes over three or four years,” he says. He also questions whether trial data sufficiently represent India’s diverse population and dengue’s geographical distribution. However, waning protection does not indicate harm. A reduction in efficacy alone does not demonstrate that later infections become more severe. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends Qdenga for children aged six to 16 in areas with high transmission but notes uncertainty about protection against DENV-3 and DENV-4 in individuals without prior infection. It advises against routine use in low-to-moderate transmission regions until further evidence is available and urges countries to consider regional transmission differences rather than applying a uniform policy. THE IMMUNITY CONCERN Dr Bagai’s most serious worry is ADE. Antibodies generated from an earlier infection may fail to neutralise a subsequent infection and can facilitate the virus’s entry into cells, increasing the risk of severe disease. Dengue is a well-known example: a second infection with a different serotype can provoke a stronger inflammatory reaction and complications. Given the wide variation in individuals’ exposure histories, Dr Bagai emphasises the need to evaluate vaccinations in this context. “If you are administering a vaccine, you must understand how the individual’s existing immune status will respond,” he states. He also suggests that prior infections such as COVID-19 and influenza might influence responses to dengue vaccination due to similarities in immune-recognition pathways. However, assertions that shared protein sequences might cause the immune system to react as if facing another dengue infection are not yet established clinical evidence of ADE following Qdenga vaccination. Such claims require specific validation. Loading... Home Photo Gallery Web Stories For You

news.title_zh: 印度登革热 疫苗 预计将于 2027 年首次接种 - Times Bull
news.source_body_en: The article from Times Bull, published on November 4, 2026, discusses the upcoming launch of the dengue vaccine Qdenga in India in 2027. The vaccine, approved by the Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO) in July 2026, is designed to target all four serotypes of the dengue virus (DENV-1 to DENV-4). It is developed using a weakened DENV-2 backbone with surface proteins from other serotypes. While the vaccine has shown efficacy of 61.2% against confirmed dengue and 84.1% against hospitalisation 4.5 years post-vaccination, it does not prevent all infections. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends its use for children aged six to 16 in high-transmission areas but highlights uncertainty about protection against DENV-3 and DENV-4 in those without prior infection. Clinicians, including Dr Sanjeev Bagai, have raised concerns about the vaccine’s effectiveness and potential risks, such as antibody-dependent enhancement (ADE), and call for further evaluation. The article also notes that dengue cases in India have increased significantly over the years, with reported cases dropping by November 2025 but likely underreported due to the disease's year-round nature and the possibility of coinfections involving multiple serotypes.

news.content: News Sports Ticket Lifestyle Real Estate Advertise Obituaries eNewspaper Legals STATE Florida dengue cases surge to 485 in largest outbreak in US in decades Cheryl McCloud C. A. Bridges USA TODAY NETWORK - Florida Oct. 30, 2026, 10:18 a.m. ET Here are symptoms of dengue fever you should watch for. How can you reduce the chances of getting mosquito-transmitted diseases in Florida? Florida reported 60 more locally acquired cases of dengue fever in one week, according to the latest update from the Florida Department of Health. The disease is also called breakbone fever, due to the pain it causes. That brings the statewide total to 485 for the year as of Oct. 24, the largest outbreak in the United States in decades. The previous highest number of Florida cases in recent memory was 199 in 2023. In 2025, Florida reported 62 cases for the year. ➤ Prevent dengue at home in Florida with this 10-minute mosquito inspection The bulk of the cases continues to be in Hillsborough County on Florida's west coast, which has 385 confirmed cases. Locally acquired cases have now been reported in 12 counties. The outbreak prompted Hillsborough County Administrator Bonnie Wise to extend a state of local emergency to Nov. 5 in the county as officials "work to control the mosquito population and protect residents from dengue fever." One death was confirmed in Hillsborough County, identified as 80-year-old Gay Small, who died of “dengue infection” along with septic shock and multi-organ failure, according to a death certificate. The previous largest outbreak was in Hawaii's Big Island, where 264 local cases were reported in the six months between September 2015 and March 2016. President Trump in September issued an order for a "campaign" to reduce the mosquito and tick population in Washington, D.C. That model could then be "applied as targeted, innovative, non-chemical pest control for the whole nation." Dengue isn't the only mosquito-transmitted disease that has popped up this year in Florida, although those have been in far fewer numbers than dengue: West Nile Virus, Chikungunya and Eastern Equine Encephalitis. Another case of West Nile Virus was reported in Sarasota County, bringing the 2026 total to seven cases, although two were asymptomatic. Here's what you should know about mosquito-borne illnesses in Florida, symptoms to watch for, and how best to prevent mosquito bites, including advice from the Florida Department of Health. 18 counties under mosquito-borne illness advisories, alerts A mosquito-borne illness advisory has been issued for the following counties: Bay Brevard Broward Holmes Leon Manatee Martin Palm Beach Polk Walton A mosquito-borne illness alert has been issued for the following counties: Alachua Citrus Duval Hillsborough Miami-Dade Orange Pasco Pinellas "A mosquito-borne illness advisory means the public should take precautions to reduce mosquito bites due to factors indicating local disease such as positive sentinels, very few presumptive or positive human cases, or other justifications," according to Sarasota County. "A mosquito-borne illness alert means that there has been heightened disease activity, a significant increase in vector (disease capable) mosquito populations, or an increase in locally-transmitted human cases. "Residents should continue to take precautions, but exercise additional caution in preventing mosquito bites." Dengue cases increasing in Florida, with more counties reporting mosquito-transmitted disease According to the Florida Department of Health, as of Oct. 24, there have been 485 cases of locally acquired cases of dengue reported in 12 counties, up from 425 cases reported Oct. 17. There have also been six positive samples of locally acquired of West Nile virus and one case of chikungunya. Dengue: 485 cases 385 in Hillsborough County 67 in Pinellas County 9 in Miami-Dade County 9 in Orange County 4 in Pasco County 3 in Citrus County 2 in Manatee County 1 in Brevard County 1 in Broward County 1 in Palm Beach County 1 in Polk County West Nile: seven cases 2 in Alachua County 1 in Duval County (asymptomatic blood donors) 1 in Holmes County 1 in Leon (asymptomatic blood donor) 1 in Sarasota County 1 in Walton County Chikungunya: 1 case 1 in Miami-Dade County Eastern Equine Encephalitis: 1 case 1 in Leon County What is Hillsborough County doing to try to control mosquitoes? A local state of emergency has been extended in Hillsborough County until Nov. 5. A state of local emergency can be in effect for only seven days, unless rescinded or extended, according to the Hillsborough County Department of Health. "Mosquito management crews are increasing treatments by air and ground because the county’s mosquito surveillance in many neighborhoods is showing dengue virus activity in the mosquito population. "Residents are encouraged to look for and eliminate standing water on their property after recent heavy rains." Residents can sign up to be notified where aerial treatment will occur in neighborhoods. You can also go to the county's website to see when and where mosquito "operations" are scheduled to take place. Trump wants mosquitoes, ticks eliminated in Washington, D.C. On Sept. 29, Trump signed an executive order to eliminate ticks and mosquitoes in Washington, D.C. The order directs the Secretary of the Interior, the Secretary of Agriculture, the Administrator of the Environmental Protection Agency, and the Administrator of General Services, along with the Secretary of Health and Human Services, to "develop and implement a campaign across Washington, D.C., to reduce invasive mosquito populations by 90 percent and the tick population by 50 percent by 2028 using safe and effective, non-chemical, and innovative technology-enabled methods. "This new model, localized to Washington, D.C., can later be applied nationwide as targeted, innovative, non-chemical pest control for the whole nation." Florida residents should take precautions to avoid mosquito-borne illnesses "Residents throughout the state should continue to take precautions from mosquito-borne illnesses by appropriately applying bug spray, avoiding areas with high mosquito populations, and wearing long pants and shirts when possible — especially during sunrise and sunset when mosquitos are most active," said Isabella White, FDOH press secretary via email Sept. 23. White said FDOH "continues to coordinate with local mosquito control partners to support surveillance and targeted response efforts in affected areas. These efforts help reduce mosquito populations, limit the risk of disease transmission, and protect residents across Florida." What are symptoms of dengue, breakbone fever? "Dengue fever can be a painful, debilitating disease but is rarely fatal," the Florida Department of Health said. Symptoms appear three to 14 days after the bite of an infected mosquito and include: sudden onset of fever severe headache eye pain muscle and joint pain (giving the disease the nickname “breakbone fever”) bleeding Gastrointestinal symptoms like vomiting and diarrhea may also be present in some cases. "Dengue fever symptoms usually last four to seven days. The disease is often diagnosed incorrectly because the symptoms are similar to influenza and other viruses," the CDC said. "Around one out of every 20 people infected by a dengue virus develops severe dengue, a life-threatening medical emergency that requires immediate medical attention," according to YaleMedicine. Why is dengue called 'breakbone fever?' Dengue is sometimes called “breakbone fever” because, in addition to fever, "it can cause severe aches and pains, especially in the legs, joints, and back," according to YaleMedicine. Dengue does not actually cause bones to break, according to YaleMedicine. Is dengue contagious? Dengue is spread by mosquitoes. Mosquitoes become infected with dengue after biting a person with the virus. Those infected mosquitoes then spread the virus to other people through bites. The Centers for Disease Control said a woman infected with the dengue virus during pregnancy could pass the virus to her fetus, causing death to the fetus, low birth weight, or premature birth. Can dengue be treated? "While there is no cure for dengue and there are no specific medications for the condition, getting adequate hydration and plenty of rest, and taking acetaminophen for pain and fever can help alleviate symptoms while the body’s immune system fights the virus," according to YaleMedicine. "In most cases, people recover from dengue within a week. For those with severe dengue, treatment by health care professionals can significantly lower the risk of death." What are the best mosquito repellents to use? According to the Florida Department of Health, repellents with the following active ingredients provide the best protection: DEET Picaridin IR3535 Oil of lemon eucalyptus Para-menthane-diol 2-undecanone, a plant-derived ingredient 'Drain and cover' helps keep mosquitoes away The FDOH offered this advice to help keep mosquitoes away from your Florida home: Drain Drain water from garbage cans, old tires, pool covers, or any other containers where water collects. Empty and clean birdbaths and pet water bowls at least once or twice a week. Protect boats and vehicles from rain with tarps that don’t accumulate water. Maintain swimming pools in good condition and ensure they are appropriately chlorinated. Empty plastic swimming pools when not in use. Cover If you must be outside when mosquitoes are active, cover up. Apply mosquito repellent to exposed skin and clothing. Use mosquito netting to protect children younger than 2 months old. Another case of West Nile Virus was reported in Sarasota County, bringing the 2026 total to seven cases, although two were asymptomatic. Here's what you should know about mosquito-borne illnesses in Florida, symptoms to watch for, and how best to prevent mosquito bites, including advice from the Florida Department of Health. 18 counties under mosquito-borne illness advisories, alerts A mosquito-borne illness advisory has been issued for the following counties: Bay Brevard Broward Holmes Leon Manatee Martin Palm Beach Polk Walton A mosquito-borne illness alert has been issued for the following counties: Alachua Citrus Duval Hillsborough Miami-Dade Orange Pasco Pinellas "A mosquito-borne illness advisory means the public should take precautions to reduce mosquito bites due to factors indicating local disease such as positive sentinels, very few presumptive or positive human cases, or other justifications," according to Sarasota County. "A mosquito-borne illness alert means that there has been heightened disease activity, a significant increase in vector (disease capable) mosquito populations, or an increase in locally-transmitted human cases. "Residents should continue to take precautions, but exercise additional caution in preventing mosquito bites." Dengue cases increasing in Florida, with more counties reporting mosquito-transmitted disease According to the Florida Department of Health, as of Oct. 24, there have been 485 cases of locally acquired cases of dengue reported in 12 counties, up from 425 cases reported Oct. 17. There have also been six positive samples of locally acquired of West Nile virus and one case of chikungunya. Dengue: 485 cases 385 in Hillsborough County 67 in Pinellas County 9 in Miami-Dade County 9 in Orange County 4 in Pasco County 3 in Citrus County 2 in Manatee County 1 in Brevard County 1 in Broward County 1 in Palm Beach County 1 in Polk County West Nile: seven cases 2 in Alachua County 1 in Duval County (asymptomatic blood donors) 1 in Holmes County 1 in Leon (asymptomatic blood donor) 1 in Sarasota County 1 in Walton County Chikungunya: 1 case 1 in Miami-Dade County Eastern Equine Encephalitis: 1 case 1 in Leon County What is Hillsborough County doing to try to control mosquitoes? A local state of emergency has been extended in Hillsborough County until Nov. 5. A state of local emergency can be in effect for only seven days, unless rescinded or extended, according to the Hillsborough County Department of Health. "Mosquito management crews are increasing treatments by air and ground because the county’s mosquito surveillance in many neighborhoods is showing dengue virus activity in the mosquito population. "Residents are encouraged to look for and eliminate standing water on their property after recent heavy rains." Residents can sign up to be notified where aerial treatment will occur in neighborhoods. You can also go to the county's website to see when and where mosquito "operations" are scheduled to take place. Trump wants mosquitoes, ticks eliminated in Washington, D.C. On Sept. 29, Trump signed an executive order to eliminate ticks and mosquitoes in Washington, D.C. The order directs the Secretary of the Interior, the Secretary of Agriculture, the Administrator of the Environmental Protection Agency, and the Administrator of General Services, along with the Secretary of Health and Human Services, to "develop and implement a campaign across Washington, D.C., to reduce invasive mosquito populations by 90 percent and the tick population by 50 percent by 2028 using safe and effective, non-chemical, and innovative technology-enabled methods. "This new model, localized to Washington, D.C., can later be applied nationwide as targeted, innovative, non-chemical pest control for the whole nation." Florida residents should take precautions to avoid mosquito-borne illnesses "Residents throughout the state should continue to take precautions from mosquito-borne illnesses by appropriately applying bug spray, avoiding areas with high mosquito populations, and wearing long pants and shirts when possible — especially during sunrise and sunset when mosquitos are most active," said Isabella White, FDOH press secretary via email Sept. 23. White said FDOH "continues to coordinate with local mosquito control partners to support surveillance and targeted response efforts in affected areas. These efforts help reduce mosquito populations, limit the risk of disease transmission, and protect residents across Florida." What are symptoms of dengue, breakbone fever? "Dengue fever can be a painful, debilitating disease but is rarely fatal," the Florida Department of Health said. Symptoms appear three to 14 days after the bite of an infected mosquito and include: sudden onset of fever severe headache eye pain muscle and joint pain (giving the disease the nickname “breakbone fever”) bleeding Gastrointestinal symptoms like vomiting and diarrhea may also be present in some cases. "Dengue fever symptoms usually last four to seven days. The disease is often diagnosed incorrectly because the symptoms are similar to influenza and other viruses," the CDC said. "Around one out of every 20 people infected by a dengue virus develops severe dengue, a life-threatening medical emergency that requires immediate medical attention," according to YaleMedicine. Why is dengue called 'breakbone fever?' Dengue is sometimes called “breakbone fever” because, in addition to fever, "it can cause severe aches and pains, especially in the legs, joints, and back," according to YaleMedicine. Dengue does not actually cause bones to break, according to YaleMedicine. Is dengue contagious? Dengue is spread by mosquitoes. Mosquitoes become infected with dengue after biting a person with the virus. Those infected mosquitoes then spread the virus to other people through bites. The Centers for Disease Control said a woman infected with the dengue virus during pregnancy could pass the virus to her fetus, causing death to the fetus, low birth weight, or premature birth. Can dengue be treated? "While there is no cure for dengue and there are no specific medications for the condition, getting adequate hydration and plenty of rest, and taking acetaminophen for pain and fever can help alleviate symptoms while the body’s immune system fights the virus," according to YaleMedicine. "In most cases, people recover from dengue within a week. For those with severe dengue, treatment by health care professionals can significantly lower the risk of death." What are the best mosquito repellents to use? According to the Florida Department of Health, repellents with the following active ingredients provide the best protection: DEET Picaridin IR3535 Oil of lemon eucalyptus Para-menthane-diol 2-undecanone, a plant-derived ingredient 'Drain and cover' helps keep mosquitoes away The FDOH offered this advice to help keep mosquitoes away from your Florida home: Drain Drain water from garbage cans, old tires, pool covers, or any other containers where water collects. Empty and clean birdbaths and pet water bowls at least once or twice a week. Protect boats and vehicles from rain with tarps that don’t accumulate water. Maintain swimming pools in good condition and ensure they are appropriately chlorinated. Empty plastic swimming pools when not in use. Cover If you must be outside when mosquitoes are active, cover up. Apply mosquito repellent to exposed skin and clothing. Use mosquito netting to protect children younger than 2 months old. While the outbreak is significant, other mosquito-transmitted diseases like West Nile virus and chikungunya have been reported in smaller numbers. The state is promoting non-chemical pest control methods to manage the situation.

news.source_body_en: Florida is experiencing its largest dengue outbreak in decades, with 485 confirmed cases as of October 24, 2026, according to the Florida Department of Health. The majority of these cases, 385, are concentrated in Hillsborough County on the west coast. The outbreak has spread to 12 counties, including Pinellas, Miami-Dade, and Orange. One death was confirmed in Hillsborough County, attributed to dengue infection, septic shock, and multi-organ failure. The state has extended a local emergency declaration until November 5, 2026, to address the mosquito population and prevent further transmission. Mosquito management crews are intensifying treatments, and residents are urged to eliminate standing water on their property. The Florida Department of Health is working with local partners to monitor and respond to the outbreak. Dengue, also known as breakbone fever, causes severe aches and pains and can be life-threatening in some cases. While the outbreak is significant, other mosquito-transmitted diseases like West Nile virus and chikungunya have been reported in smaller numbers. The state is promoting non-chemical pest control methods to manage the situation.
news.content_zh: 据佛罗里达州卫生部称,佛罗里达州正在经历数十年来最大规模的登革热 暴发,截至 2026 年 10 月 24 日,已有 485 例确诊病例。其中大部分病例(385 例)集中在西海岸的希尔斯伯勒县。暴发 已蔓延到 12 个县,包括皮内拉斯、迈阿密戴德县和奥兰治。希尔斯伯勒县确认一例死亡,原因是登革热感染、感染性休克和多器官衰竭。该州已将当地紧急状态声明延长至 2026 年 11 月 5 日,以解决蚊子数量问题并防止进一步的 传播。灭蚊人员正在加强治疗,并敦促居民清除其房产上的积水。佛罗里达州卫生部正在与当地合作伙伴合作,监测和应对 暴发。登革热也称为断骨热,会引起剧烈疼痛,在某些情况下可能危及生命。虽然 暴发 很重要,但西尼罗河病毒和基孔肯雅热等其他蚊子传播疾病的报告数量较少。国家正在推广非化学害虫防治方法来控制这种情况。

Health & Wellness Sports Hustle 11.03.26 | Home Health & Wellness Florida’s mosquito problem has taken a historic turn and three counties are now under emergency declarations Emergency declarations enabled regional health officials to coordinate rapid vector control operations following the largest locally acquired dengue outbreak recorded since 1930. Local government agencies across the Tampa Bay area intensified ground and aerial larvicide treatments to suppress infected mosquito populations within residential zones. Public health specialists urge residents to recognize critical warning signs early while actively eliminating standing water sources around private properties. Unprecedented health alerts expanded rapidly across the state after official CDC reporting confirmed during a technical presentation on October 22, 2026, that Florida’s mosquito population triggered the largest dengue outbreak since the 1930s; furthermore, data compiled through October 15 detailed 368 autochthonous cases across 8 counties alongside 288 travel cases, while field inspectors identified 20 virus positive mosquito pools and registered that 47% of infected local patients required immediate hospitalization alongside 1 confirmed death: “This represents the most significant local dengue transmission cycle in state history.” Meanwhile, accelerating vector proliferation affected urban communities surrounding Tampa Bay, with Hillsborough County emerging as the primary epicenter; consequently, public health entomologists confirmed that Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus species continue breeding aggressively in artificial water containers, prompting regional environmental health departments to issue urgent epidemiological advisories across affected neighborhoods. Vector control operations and emergency declarations in affected jurisdictions Local government commissions in Hillsborough, Pasco, and Pinellas approved emergency declarations during the final week of September; specifically, Pasco ratified its initial resolution on September 23 while Hillsborough and Pinellas enacted parallel measures on September 24, streamlining administrative procurement procedures and unlocking emergency funding for immediate ground spraying operations without establishing general movement restrictions. In addition, extending these special powers through late October, official county health communications verified that administrators prolonged emergency status from October 29 through November 5 while Pinellas extended its resolution on October 22 through October 29 to ensure reimbursement access; as a result, these operational frameworks allowed Pinellas authorities to coordinate directly with Lee County Mosquito Control to execute targeted aerial larvicide applications over critical zones in St. Petersburg and Clearwater. ¿Tienes HIV, Mijo? In parallel, scaling up field interventions under continuous emergency declarations, environmental health teams expanded door to door property inspections and localized ultra low volume barrier sprays; simultaneously, municipal administrators instructed property owners to grant access to control technicians while actively removing stagnant water receptacles from residential yards. Preventive protocols and emergency declarations guidelines for community safety Outlining essential community protection guidelines under current emergency declarations, public health officials published mandatory protection guidelines for all residents: EPA registered insect repellents: Health experts recommend formulations containing DEET or picaridin to prevent bites from Florida’s mosquito. Elimination of standing water: Homeowners must drain standing water receptacles weekly to prevent conditions requiring emergency declarations. Protective outdoor clothing: Individuals should wear loose long sleeved shirts and pants during day and night hours. Immediate medical evaluation: Severe abdominal pain or mucosal bleeding requires immediate emergency medical evaluation. Residential inspection clearance: Residents must grant full access to vector control teams evaluating local vector breeding sites. Clinical management and severe dengue symptom surveillance under emergency declarations Clinical manifestations of dengue fever typically present as high fever accompanied by headache, retro orbital pain, muscle aches, nausea, vomiting and rash lasting between 2 and 7 days; nevertheless, medical specialists warn that the critical phase of severe dengue often begins precisely when the acute fever starts to subside after approximately 1 week. In response to potential complications while municipal authorities enforce emergency declarations, CDC guidelines emphasize immediate hospital admission upon detecting warning signs such as abdominal tenderness or blood in vomit and stool; for this reason, regional emergency rooms maintain active clinical surveillance to deliver timely fluid management and protect residents from the health risks associated with Florida’s mosquito. analysis.time: The outbreak was confirmed on October 22, 2026, with emergency declarations approved during the final week of September 2026 and extended through late October 2026. The event date range is from September 23 to October 29, 2026, with ongoing activities through November 5, 2026.
analysis.location_and_population: The outbreak primarily affected the Tampa Bay metropolitan area, specifically Hillsborough, Pasco, and Pinellas counties in Florida. The affected population includes residents of these counties, with a focus on urban communities and private property owners.
analysis.event: Florida experienced its largest locally acquired dengue outbreak since the 1930s, with emergency declarations issued by Hillsborough, Pasco, and Pinellas counties. The outbreak was confirmed by the CDC during a technical presentation on October 22, 2026, and included 368 autochthonous cases across 8 counties and 288 travel cases.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The outbreak recorded 456 confirmed local cases across 3 counties, with 385 in Hillsborough, 67 in Pinellas, and 4 in Pasco. The outbreak is described as the most significant local dengue transmission cycle in state history.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: Emergency declarations were approved in late September 2026 and extended through late October 2026. Vector control operations, including ground and aerial larvicide treatments, were intensified. Public health officials issued epidemiological advisories and preventive guidelines, urging residents to eliminate standing water and use protective measures.

analysis.brief_en: Florida is facing its largest dengue outbreak since the 1930s, with three counties—Hillsborough, Pasco, and Pinellas—declaring emergencies to manage the crisis. The outbreak was confirmed by the CDC on October 22, 2026, and included 368 autochthonous cases across 8 counties and 288 travel cases. The Tampa Bay metropolitan area was the primary epicenter, with 456 confirmed local cases reported by October 30, 2026. Public health officials emphasized the need for rapid vector control operations, including intensified larvicide treatments and property inspections. Preventive measures such as eliminating standing water and using EPA-approved insect repellents were recommended to mitigate the spread. The outbreak has led to 47% of local patients requiring hospitalization and one confirmed death, prompting urgent health alerts and community safety guidelines. Emergency declarations allowed for streamlined administrative procedures and access to emergency funding, with ongoing efforts to control the mosquito population and prevent further transmission.
