Home El Bajío El Bajío News MND Local Guadalajara: How the water crisis is affecting local businesses, fewer dengue cases and a new ‘Made in Jalisco’ seal By Dawn Stoner November 2, 2026 0 Dengue cases are down significantly in Jalisco, but Guadalajara's ongoing water crisis continues to prompt warnings. (Kenneth Lopez/Unsplash) This past week, business leaders and government officials sparred over whether the ongoing water crisis in the Guadalajara Metro Area (GMA) will affect business investment in Jalisco, so we looked at the facts. Meanwhile, as the rainy season winds down, dengue cases have fallen sharply across the state compared to 2025, and a new “Hecho en Jalisco” (“Made in Jalisco”) seal aims to boost the visibility and cachet of select local products. Business leader warns investment will suffer due to water quality issues José Medina Mora, president of the Business Coordinating Council, believes the ongoing water crisis in Guadalajara will slow investment in Jalisco. (Graciela López/Cuartoscuro) Speaking to local journalists on Oct. 23, José Medina Mora, president of the Business Coordinating Council (CCE), issued a stark warning to Jalisco state officials. Medina Mora said he expects investment projects in Jalisco to be negatively impacted by Guadalajara’s ongoing water crisis, noting, “There will be investment decisions in Jalisco, and in Guadalajara particularly, that will be halted until we can offer quality water.” Medina Mora also blamed local politicians for their failure to anticipate and solve these issues before they became acute. Jalisco governor details US $1.3B investment in Guadalajara’s water infrastructure: Wednesday’s mañanera recapped Later clarifying his comments, Medina Mora said the CCE does not expect the water crisis to spark capital flight from Jalisco but expects new investments to be put on hold due to the increased business risk posed by water contamination. State and federal government officials swiftly pushed back on Medina Mora’s comments. Government points to strong FDI as local businesses adapt Ximena Escobedo Juárez, undersecretary of industry at the Ministry of Industry and Commerce of the Ministry of Economy, cited strong business investment across Jalisco in 2026 as evidence that the business community remains undeterred. The ongoing water crisis in the GMA has reached the point where officials will be shutting down the parts of the system most responsible for the dirty water and rationing the reduced supply until replacements are built and operating. (Fernando Carranza García / Cuartoscuro.com) In the first half of 2026, Jalisco attracted US $1.41 billion in new capital, surpassing the US $1.2 billion invested in the state for all of 2025. This contrasts with a sharp decline in foreign direct investment in Mexico’s first half overall. Yet some economic disruption is undeniable. With municipal water supplies being rationed over the next six months, many local businesses are scrambling to arrange deliveries from private water trucks to avoid major disruptions to area restaurants, hotels, hospitals and other local service providers. In addition, manufacturers around Guadalajara have reportedly been supplementing operations with more sophisticated filtration protocols, including on-site chlorination systems, sediment micro-filters and reverse osmosis units. These enhancements are needed to remove heavy metals, sediment and fecal matter from the municipal water that enters their facilities and keep contaminated water from damaging their industrial equipment. Rainy season ebbs with dengue cases in Jalisco down by 90% Through Oct. 11, Jalisco has 242 confirmed dengue cases in 2026, ranking 12th nationwide . This represents a massive improvement over 2025, when Jalisco ranked third nationwide for dengue, behind Sonora and Veracruz. Year to date, there have been two confirmed deaths, with five more under investigation. Last year, the state recorded 10 dengue deaths. Dengue cases in Jalisco Year Confirmed Cases Percent change, year over year 2023 941 N/A 2024 20,907 2,122% 2025 2,317 -89% 2026 (through Oct. 11) 242 -90% Source: Secretaría de Salud Some strains of dengue are more virulent than others. One of the serotypes that is spreading in Jalisco right now is the most virulent form (serotype 2), which causes dengue hemorrhagic fever. Year to date, both serotypes 2 and 3 of the virus are circulating in Jalisco. It is a mistake to think that most people get infected with dengue in remote, jungle areas. Rapid urbanization and increased population density have created conditions ideal for mosquito breeding and infection. Yordi Raúl Portillo Montes, who heads Jalisco’s National Public Health Service, noted that the highest incidence of dengue in the state has occurred in Cocula and Teuchitlán, with coastal areas, including Puerto Vallarta, also at high risk. In the GMA, central Guadalajara, Tonalá and Tlaquepaque have recorded the most cases this year. While dengue is less common outside of the rainy season, the risk does not fall to zero. Due to the water crisis affecting Guadalajara, hundreds of families have resorted to storing water in buckets, drums or other containers, which has increased dengue risk in urban areas. In response, health authorities have reiterated the importance of covering these containers to discourage mosquito breeding. While there is a vaccine for dengue, it can be difficult to access in Mexico, so your best bet is to be proactive and avoid infection. The new ‘Made in Jalisco’ seal aims to promote and protect local products View this post on Instagram A post shared by Secretaría de Desarrollo Económico Jalisco (@sedeco.jalisco) In a bid to strengthen the marketing of products made in the state, the Jalisco Ministry of Economic Development (Sedeco) recently announced the launch of the “Made in Jalisco” seal . The initiative aims to increase visibility for Jalisco-made products with protected designations in foreign markets while ensuring that the economic benefits flow through to local communities where they are made. The new seal is expected to recognize at least 40 businesses that make products with a designation of origin or geographical indication. Participation will be free, and eligible businesses include companies, cooperatives, workshops and individual producers of tequila, raicilla, Yahualica chili or Sayula cajeta that have authorization from the Mexican Institute of Industrial Property (IMPI). Agave: The noble plant at the heart of Mexican culture However, the Jalisco Ministry of Economic Development (Sedeco) and the civil association El Telar will decide which products are eligible to display the new seal. Applicants will be judged on their history and roots in Jalisco, their products’ distinctive qualities, organizational preparedness and desire for designation of origin protection. According to state figures, the tequila supply chain supports more than 100,000 families, while raicilla involves more than 80 artisanal producers. Yahualica chili peppers are cultivated by roughly 250 small farmers and collectives, and Sayula cajeta is produced in 21 family workshops. MND writer Dawn Stoner is reporting from Guadalajara. Mexico-Canada trade was up more than 18% through August MND Staff - November 3, 2026 0 Trade in goods between the two North American countries was worth 34.42 billion Canadian dollars (CAD) in the first eight months of 2026, a year-over-year increase of 18.3%. news.content: Uzbekistan World Politics Crime Culture Sport Health Lifestyle ENG +12°C 1 USD = 11,975 World 21:57 / 31.10.2026 Share Dengue epidemic worsens in Bangladesh: 418 people have died Experts forecast that the epidemic will continue in November as well, and the situation will not improve even until December. Bangladesh is experiencing a worsening dengue fever epidemic. Since the beginning of the year, 418 people have died from the disease, and more than 133,000 patients have been hospitalized. Experts report that virus transmission may continue through November, with a significant decline unlikely to be observed until December. According to the country's Ministry of Health, 173 people died from dengue fever in October. This is more than the 148 deaths recorded in September, making it the month with the highest death toll so far in 2026. At the same time, the country is also battling the world's largest measles epidemic. This disease has claimed the lives of more than 1,200 people. The simultaneous spread of two epidemics is placing an additional burden on Bangladesh's healthcare system. Doctors say that many patients seek hospital care only after the disease has begun to cause severe complications. At Shahid Suhrawardy Medical College and Hospital in Dhaka, 279 patients with dengue fever are being treated. Another 67 people were admitted to the facility in a single day. Experts emphasize that reinfection, as well as delays in diagnosis and treatment, are increasing the risk of severe cases. Because all four serotypes of the dengue virus are circulating in the country, a person previously infected can be reinfected with a different serotype and face severe complications. According to the forecast of Jahangirnagar University entomologist Kabirul Bashar, the incidence may decrease somewhat in November, but virus transmission will continue. In his view, there is a high probability that significant improvement will not be observed until December. The expert explained this by the fact that previous rainfall has created favorable breeding sites for mosquitoes. In addition, changes in rainfall and humidity patterns due to climate change are extending the mosquito breeding season. The country continues to face the spread of the disease after recording the highest monthly death toll in October. According to data from the "Directorate General of Health Services" reported by "BD News 24" on Sunday, the total number of hospital admissions due to the disease reached 136,929 cases since the beginning of the year, with 130,388 patients discharged after receiving treatment. The data indicated that October recorded 174 deaths from dengue fever, making it the month with the highest deaths since the beginning of the year, compared to 148 deaths in September. The "Daily Star" reported, based on official health data, that 6,114 patients are still receiving treatment in hospitals across the country. Dhaka Division recorded the highest number of new hospital admissions, with 831 cases from Saturday morning to Sunday morning, followed by Khulna Division with 259 cases, and Chittagong with 257 cases. Other cases were distributed across Barisal Division with 213 cases, Rajshahi with 185 cases, Mymensingh with 92 cases, Rangpur with 73 cases, and Sylhet with 19 cases, reflecting the spread of the disease in various regions of the country. The official figures refer to hospital admissions and do not necessarily include all dengue fever cases, as some infections may go unnoticed or present mild symptoms not requiring hospitalization. Bangladesh's health authorities have been maintaining records of admissions and deaths related to dengue fever since 2000. The country experienced its worst recorded outbreak of the disease in 2023, when the number of hospital admissions reached 321,179, with 1,705 deaths, according to data from "BD News 24". Despite the rise in deaths last October, the recorded toll since the beginning of 2026 remains lower than the figures during the outbreak in 2023. Dengue fever is a viral disease primarily transmitted to humans through the bites of infected Aedes mosquitoes, and it particularly spreads in tropical and subtropical regions. The "World Health Organization" estimates that about half of the world's population is at risk of contracting the disease, with an estimated 100 million to 400 million infections occurring annually worldwide. The organization clarifies that most infections do not cause symptoms or result in mild symptoms, although some cases may develop into severe disease that poses life-threatening risks. Common symptoms include fever, headache, body aches, nausea, and rash, while signs of severe infection may appear after fever subsides. Key danger signs include severe abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, rapid breathing, and bleeding, which are symptoms requiring urgent medical care. The "World Health Organization" emphasizes that early diagnosis and provision of proper medical care contribute to reducing deaths due to severe cases, even though there is no specific treatment that eliminates the virus itself. According to the "Centers for Disease Control and Prevention", four closely related viral serotypes can cause dengue fever, meaning that recovery from a previous infection does not provide complete protection against subsequent infections. (WWSB) - Health officials have confirmed a second locally acquired dengue case in Manatee County. The Florida Department of Health in Manatee County announced the update Friday, one week after WWSB reported the county’s first publicly announced locally acquired dengue case. DOH-Manatee said it is working with county departments and Manatee County Mosquito Control on increased surveillance and prevention efforts. The work includes truck fogging, aerial larviciding and localized inspections for mosquito breeding areas. The department did not identify where either person may have been exposed. It also did not release the patients’ conditions, say whether the cases are connected or provide dates and locations for mosquito-control treatments. Dengue fever case confirmed in Manatee County as cases rise across Florida Manatee County confirms locally acquired dengue case Dengue is spread through the bite of an infected Aedes aegypti mosquito, according to the health department. It is not spread person-to-person. Symptoms can include fever, severe muscle and joint pain, and sometimes a rash. The department says symptoms can appear within 15 days after a bite from an infected mosquito. Health officials are asking residents to reduce mosquito bites and breeding areas around their homes. Recommended steps include wearing loose-fitting long sleeves and pants, applying EPA-registered insect repellent, repairing damaged window and door screens, and draining standing water from containers such as buckets, pool covers, coolers, toys and flowerpots. Anyone with symptoms should contact a health care provider, according to DOH-Manatee. Copyright 2026 WWSB. All rights reserved. news.content: News Sports Ticket Lifestyle Real Estate Advertise Obituaries eNewspaper Legals SARASOTA Manatee confirms second local dengue case amid Florida surge Manatee County confirms its second locally acquired dengue case as Florida infections surge. Wade Tatangelo Sarasota Herald-Tribune Oct. 30, 2026, 12:31 p.m. ET Manatee County has confirmed its second locally acquired case of dengue as Florida experiences a surge in the mosquito-borne illness. The Florida Department of Health in Manatee County announced the new case Oct. 30, saying health officials have been working with Manatee County departments and Manatee County Mosquito Control on increased surveillance and prevention efforts. Those efforts include increased truck fogging, aerial larvicide treatments and ground inspections for locations where mosquitoes could be breeding. The Manatee County case comes amid a sharp rise in dengue infections across Florida. The state has reported 485 dengue cases, according to previously published USA TODAY Network - Florida reporting. Dengue is transmitted through the bite of an infected Aedes aegypti mosquito. The disease is not contagious from person to person. Symptoms can resemble the flu and include fever, severe muscle and joint pain and, in some cases, a rash. Respiratory symptoms generally are not associated with dengue. Symptoms can appear within 15 days after a person is bitten by an infected mosquito, according to the Florida Department of Health. Health officials are urging Manatee County residents to take precautions to avoid mosquito bites. Residents should wear loose-fitting, long-sleeved shirts and pants and use insect repellents registered by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency on exposed skin and clothing. EPA-registered repellents are considered safe and effective when used as directed, including for pregnant and breastfeeding women, according to health officials. Residents also should eliminate standing water around their homes that can provide mosquito breeding grounds. Officials recommend draining water from garbage cans, buckets, pool covers, coolers, toys, flowerpots and other containers where rainwater or sprinkler water can collect. Damaged screens on windows, doors, porches and patios also should be repaired to help prevent mosquitoes from getting inside. The Florida Department of Health conducts statewide surveillance for mosquito-borne illnesses, including dengue, West Nile virus, Eastern equine encephalitis, St. Louis encephalitis, malaria and chikungunya. Anyone experiencing symptoms of dengue should contact a health care provider. Wade Tatangelo is the executive editor of the Sarasota Herald-Tribune and Florida dining and entertainment editor for the USA TODAY Network. Follow him on Facebook, Instagram, and X. He can be reached by email at wade.tatangelo@heraldtribune.com. Support local journalism by subscribing. news.source_body_en: Manatee County, Florida, confirmed its second locally acquired case of dengue on October 30, 2026, at 12:31 p.m. ET, amid a surge in dengue infections across the state, which has reported 485 cases. The Florida Department of Health stated that health officials are collaborating with local departments and mosquito control to enhance surveillance and prevention measures. These efforts include increased truck fogging, aerial larvicide treatments, and ground inspections to identify mosquito breeding sites. Officials are also urging residents to take precautions such as wearing long-sleeved clothing, using EPA-registered insect repellents, and eliminating standing water around homes to reduce mosquito populations. Dengue is transmitted through the bite of an infected Aedes aegypti mosquito and is not contagious from person to person. Symptoms can include fever, severe muscle and joint pain, and a rash, typically appearing within 15 days of a bite. Residents are advised to contact healthcare providers if they experience symptoms of dengue.

Got it Edition CA NY US News Metro Long Island Politics World News Search Search Recommended Skip to main content California News Vicious ‘ankle biter’ mosquitoes capable of spreading dengue fever invade California coastal city By Sheetal Banchariya Published Nov. 3, 2026, 3:43 p.m. ET 55 Comments See more of our coverage in your search results. Make California Post a Preferred Source 1/1 Skip Ad Continue watchingafter the adVisit Advertiser websiteGO TO PAGE These mosquitoes don’t wait for dusk and go straight for your ankles! Yellow fever mosquitoes native to Sub-Saharan Africa have been wreaking havoc in several neighborhoods of picturesque coastal areas in Southern California. Santa Barbara County’s Mosquito and Vector Management District confirmed that four ‘Aedes aegypti’ blood-suckers were found on Oct. 30 near North Voluntario and East Cota streets. Residents tormented by the mosquitoes have named them “ankle biters.” SILVIA MAQQ – stock.adobe.com The agency said a total of four ‘Aedes aegypti’ mosquitoes, capable of causing dengue fever, were trapped in different locations across Santa Barbara last week. Two were found near North Voluntario and Cota streets, one at Laguna and East Carrillo, and one near East Victoria and Olive. According to the District, the same species was found Oct. 20 in the eastern Goleta Valley, near Turnpike Road and Calle Real, and in Carpinteria in July. A second non-native species is already in town. Australian backyard mosquitoes, ‘Aedes notoscriptus,’ were found in Santa Barbara’s West Side in March and in the Mesa neighborhood in June. Both species like to bite around the feet and ankles, and they do it during the day, indoors and out. Residents tormented by the pests have named them “ankle biters.” “Please contact the District if you find yourself being bitten by aggressive mosquitoes indoors or outdoors during daytime hours,” the agency said, asking residents to call 805-969-5050 or send a message through the “Contact Us” page on its website. Dengue fever is often accompanied by severe body aches, giving it the nickname “breakbone fever.” According to the Mayo Clinic, individuals typically display symptoms 4 to 10 days after being bitten by an infected mosquito Australian backyard mosquitoes, ‘Aedes notoscriptus,’ were found in Santa Barbara’s West Side in March. Getty Images Santa Barbara’s troubles come as the whole region swelters through what many residents call a year of agony. Record-shattering heat waves and El Niño threats have turned Southern California into a breeding paradise for the winged pests. “I’ve been here my whole life and the amount of mosquitoes I’ve seen this summer has been insane,” one woman said in a TikTok video that has drawn more than 21,000 likes. 5 What do you think? Post a comment. Los Angeles County has recorded over 180 cases of West Nile virus this year—the highest spike in nearly a decade, according to the local public health department. The region’s native ‘Culex’ mosquito picks up West Nile from wild birds before passing it on to humans. In nearby Orange County, vector control officials have pulled a staggering 850 traps loaded with West Nile-positive bugs, reports the Guardian. supplementary_news.content: Mock Drafts Positional Rankings NFL News Odds Betting Newsletter STATE Florida dengue cases surge to 485 in largest outbreak in US in decades Cheryl McCloud C. A. Bridges USA TODAY NETWORK - Florida Oct. 30, 2026, 10:18 a.m. ET Here are symptoms of dengue fever you should watch for. How can you reduce the chances of getting mosquito-transmitted diseases in Florida? Florida reported 60 more locally acquired cases of dengue fever in one week, according to the latest update from the Florida Department of Health. The disease is also called breakbone fever, due to the pain it causes. That brings the statewide total to 485 for the year as of Oct. 24, the largest outbreak in the United States in decades. The previous highest number of Florida cases in recent memory was 199 in 2023. In 2025, Florida reported 62 cases for the year. ➤ Prevent dengue at home in Florida with this 10-minute mosquito inspection The bulk of the cases continues to be in Hillsborough County on Florida's west coast, which has 385 confirmed cases. Locally acquired cases have now been reported in 12 counties. The outbreak prompted Hillsborough County Administrator Bonnie Wise to extend a state of local emergency to Nov. 5 in the county as officials "work to control the mosquito population and protect residents from dengue fever." One death was confirmed in Hillsborough County, identified as 80-year-old Gay Small, who died of “dengue infection” along with septic shock and multi-organ failure, according to a death certificate. The previous largest outbreak was in Hawaii's Big Island, where 264 local cases were reported in the six months between September 2015 and March 2016. President Trump in September issued an order for a "campaign" to reduce the mosquito and tick population in Washington, D.C. That model could then be "applied as targeted, innovative, non-chemical pest control for the whole nation." Dengue isn't the only mosquito-transmitted disease that has popped up this year in Florida, although those have been in far fewer numbers than dengue: West Nile Virus, Chikungunya and Eastern Equine Encephalitis. Another case of West Nile Virus was reported in Sarasota County, bringing the 2026 total to seven cases, although two were asymptomatic. Here's what you should know about mosquito-borne illnesses in Florida, symptoms to watch for, and how best to prevent mosquito bites, including advice from the Florida Department of Health. 18 counties under mosquito-borne illness advisories, alerts A mosquito-borne illness advisory has been issued for the following counties: Bay Brevard Broward Holmes Leon Manatee Martin Palm Beach Polk Walton A mosquito-borne illness alert has been issued for the following counties: Alachua Citrus Duval Hillsborough Miami-Dade Orange Pasco Pinellas "A mosquito-borne illness advisory means the public should take precautions to reduce mosquito bites due to factors indicating local disease such as positive sentinels, very few presumptive or positive human cases, or other justifications," according to Sarasota County. "A mosquito-borne illness alert means that there has been heightened disease activity, a significant increase in vector (disease capable) mosquito populations, or an increase in locally-transmitted human cases. "Residents should continue to take precautions, but exercise additional caution in preventing mosquito bites." Dengue cases increasing in Florida, with more counties reporting mosquito-transmitted disease According to the Florida Department of Health, as of Oct. 24, there have been 485 cases of locally acquired cases of dengue reported in 12 counties, up from 425 cases reported Oct. 17. There have also been six positive samples of locally acquired of West Nile virus and one case of chikungunya. Dengue: 485 cases 385 in Hillsborough County 67 in Pinellas County 9 in Miami-Dade County 9 in Orange County 4 in Pasco County 3 in Citrus County 2 in Manatee County 1 in Brevard County 1 in Broward County 1 in Palm Beach County 1 in Polk County West Nile: seven cases 2 in Alachua County 1 in Duval County (asymptomatic blood donors) 1 in Holmes County 1 in Leon (asymptomatic blood donor) 1 in Sarasota County 1 in Walton County Chikungunya: 1 case 1 in Miami-Dade County Eastern Equine Encephalitis: 1 case 1 in Leon County What is Hillsborough County doing to try to control mosquitoes? A local state of emergency has been extended in Hillsborough County until Nov. 5. A state of local emergency can be in effect for only seven days, unless rescinded or extended, according to the Hillsborough County Department of Health. "Mosquito management crews are increasing treatments by air and ground because the county’s mosquito surveillance in many neighborhoods is showing dengue virus activity in the mosquito population. "Residents are encouraged to look for and eliminate standing water on their property after recent heavy rains." Residents can sign up to be notified where aerial treatment will occur in neighborhoods. You can also go to the county's website to see when and where mosquito "operations" are scheduled to take place. Trump wants mosquitoes, ticks eliminated in Washington, D.C. On Sept. 29, Trump signed an executive order to eliminate ticks and mosquitoes in Washington, D.C. The order directs the Secretary of the Interior, the Secretary of Agriculture, the Administrator of the Environmental Protection Agency, and the Administrator of General Services, along with the Secretary of Health and Human Services, to "develop and implement a campaign across Washington, D.C., to reduce invasive mosquito populations by 90 percent and the tick population by 50 percent by 2028 using safe and effective, non-chemical, and innovative technology-enabled methods. "This new model, localized to Washington, D.C., can later be applied nationwide as targeted, innovative, non-chemical pest control for the whole nation." Florida residents should take precautions to avoid mosquito-borne illnesses "Residents throughout the state should continue to take precautions from mosquito-borne illnesses by appropriately applying bug spray, avoiding areas with high mosquito populations, and wearing long pants and shirts when possible — especially during sunrise and sunset when mosquitos are most active," said Isabella White, FDOH press secretary via email Sept. 23. White said FDOH "continues to coordinate with local mosquito control partners to support surveillance and targeted response efforts in affected areas. These efforts help reduce mosquito populations, limit the risk of disease transmission, and protect residents across Florida." What are symptoms of dengue, breakbone fever? "Dengue fever can be a painful, debilitating disease but is rarely fatal," the Florida Department of Health said. Symptoms appear three to 14 days after the bite of an infected mosquito and include: sudden onset of fever severe headache eye pain muscle and joint pain (giving the disease the nickname “breakbone fever”) bleeding Gastrointestinal symptoms like vomiting and diarrhea may also be present in some cases. "Dengue fever symptoms usually last four to seven days. The disease is often diagnosed incorrectly because the symptoms are similar to influenza and other viruses," the CDC said. "Around one out of every 20 people infected by a dengue virus develops severe dengue, a life-threatening medical emergency that requires immediate medical attention," according to YaleMedicine. Why is dengue called 'breakbone fever?' Dengue is sometimes called “breakbone fever” because, in addition to fever, "it can cause severe aches and pains, especially in the legs, joints, and back," according to YaleMedicine. Dengue does not actually cause bones to break, according to YaleMedicine. Is dengue contagious? Dengue is spread by mosquitoes. Mosquitoes become infected with dengue after biting a person with the virus. Those infected mosquitoes then spread the virus to other people through bites. The Centers for Disease Control said a woman infected with the dengue virus during pregnancy could pass the virus to her fetus, causing death to the fetus, low birth weight, or premature birth. Can dengue be treated? "While there is no cure for dengue and there are no specific medications for the condition, getting adequate hydration and plenty of rest, and taking acetaminophen for pain and fever can help alleviate symptoms while the body’s immune system fights the virus," according to YaleMedicine. "In most cases, people recover from dengue within a week. For those with severe dengue, treatment by health care professionals can significantly lower the risk of death." What are the best mosquito repellents to use? According to the Florida Department of Health, repellents with the following active ingredients provide the best protection: DEET Picaridin IR3535 Oil of lemon eucalyptus Para-menthane-diol 2-undecanone, a plant-derived ingredient 'Drain and cover' helps keep mosquitoes away The FDOH offered this advice to help keep mosquitoes away from your Florida home: Drain Drain water from garbage cans, old tires, pool covers, or any other containers where water collects. Empty and clean birdbaths and pet water bowls at least once or twice a week. Protect boats and vehicles from rain with tarps that don’t accumulate water. Maintain swimming pools in good condition and ensure they are appropriately chlorinated. Empty plastic swimming pools when not in use. Cover If you must be outside when mosquitoes are active, cover up. Apply mosquito repellent to exposed skin and clothing. Use mosquito netting to protect children younger than 2 months old. FOX 13's Ariel Plasencia reports. The Brief Hillsborough County's local state of emergency is in effect through Thursday as local dengue fever cases climb to 385, including one reported death. County officials say aggressive treatments are showing success, with mosquito traps testing negative for dengue and some neighborhoods reporting a drastic reduction in the disease-carrying Aedes aegypti mosquito. Following a rainy weekend, health officials urge residents to dump standing water, wear bug spray, and cover up. TAMPA, Fla. - With dengue fever cases nearing 400 in Hillsborough County, the local state of emergency has been extended through this Thursday, Nov. 5. Declaring a state of local emergency gives the county access to state resources and also provides a path for reimbursement of certain expenses. Following a rainy Halloween weekend across the Tampa Bay area, mosquito control officials are urging residents to be diligent about checking their properties and dumping out any standing water. "With these active rainstorms that are coming into the region that we've seen over the weekend, mosquitoes still love that. They still love water. They still love the humidity that we're seeing. Temperatures haven't cooled down quite yet," Hillsborough County Mosquito Management senior environmental scientist Paolo Pecora told FOX 13. "So we're asking the public just to be conscious out there." Tampa Bay area dengue fever data By the numbers: According to the most recent data from the state health department, here’s how the Bay Area stacks up in total dengue cases: Hillsborough: 385 (1 reported death) Pinellas: 67 Pasco: 4 Manatee: 2 Polk: 1 Symptoms of dengue fever include fever, joint pain, and muscle aches, though it is possible to be infected and not show any symptoms. Mosquito treatments What they're saying: Despite the high case count, there is positive news in the fight against the virus. County officials say their aggressive treatment strategies — which include helicopter and truck spraying operations — are working. Mosquito traps in Hillsborough County continue to test negative for dengue. "We want to knock down the adult mosquitoes that are actively spreading the virus, and then also we want to make sure that we're eliminating the offspring," Pecora said. Additionally, targeted areas have seen a drastic reduction in the overall number of mosquitoes. Pecora told FOX 13 the East Lake area is reporting a 97% reduction in the Aedes aegypti mosquito, the specific species that spreads dengue fever. With nicer weather leading to more outdoor gatherings, officials ask that residents continue taking proper precautions by wearing bug spray, putting on long sleeves, and eliminating all standing water around their homes. "We definitely had our eyes and ears up looking at this weekend," Pecora added. "We're going to look at the rates from this week and follow up on all of our trap counts and other locations that are of concern." supplementary_news.content: News Health Four dengue cases detected in Rawalpindi in two days — Dawn UA.NEWS 01 November 2026 06:57 In Rawalpindi, Pakistan, four new dengue cases have been confirmed over the past two days. Since the start of the current season, the number of registered patients has reached 83, Dawn reports . According to district disease prevention officer Dr Jawad, three positive serological test results for the dengue virus were received on Friday and one more on Saturday. Seven people were in the dengue ward at Holy Family Hospital. Season statistics In October, 51 cases were registered in Rawalpindi, while 27 were recorded in September. No dengue cases were registered in August. As of October 31, 2026, 83 cases had been confirmed in Rawalpindi, compared with 1,586 during the same period last year. More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram . Dr Jawad also said that the dengue control campaign had been intensified in the areas from which the patients came. New cases were detected among residents of the urban part of Rawalpindi, the Union Council Wah area and Chakri. Increased surveillance The local administration ordered an immediate strengthening of field surveillance. At a meeting of the district dengue response committee, officials reviewed patients' condition, internal and external monitoring, mosquito larva detection, measures in disease hotspots and the work of field teams. Additional Deputy Commissioner for Social Services Fazail Mudassar said that negligence, absenteeism and reporting of fictitious measures as part of dengue prevention would not be tolerated, and action must be taken against those responsible immediately. 1 Health 29 wards at very high risk as dengue could turn severe in Dhaka South Staff Correspondent Published: 04 November 2026, 19:08 শেয়ার করুন: Graphics: Agamir Somoy Authorities have expressed concern that the spread of dengue and chikungunya could take a severe turn in areas under the Dhaka South City Corporation (DSCC). A joint survey by DSCC and the Communicable Disease Control (CDC) unit found on Wednesday that mosquito density in all 75 wards of DSCC exceeds the normal index. Of these, 29 wards have been classified as being at very high risk. Aedes mosquitoes were found to breed most frequently in regular residential houses and high-rise buildings rather than under construction or semi pucca buildings. The 12-day survey was conducted from September 27 to October 8 by 36 field workers from DSCC and the Communicable Disease Control (CDC) unit of the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS). The Kobo Toolbox technology was used to ensure accurate data collection. Using scientific and random sampling methods, the survey teams visited 2,250 houses, selecting 30 houses from each of DSCC’s 75 wards. After completing the survey, the collected data were analyzed to identify potential dengue hotspots. The survey found Aedes mosquito larvae and pupae in 803 of the 2,250 houses inspected. Individual houses accounted for the largest share of breeding sources, with larvae found in 31.37 percent of them. Larvae were also found in 31.06 percent of high-rise buildings, 17.39 percent of semi pucca houses, 14.11 percent of vacant plots and 13.04 percent of buildings under construction. Among the containers and locations where larvae were found, stagnant water on floors accounted for the highest share at 12.26 percent. Buckets accounted for 10.34 percent and plastic drums for 8.89 percent. Based on larval density, DSCC classified 29 wards as very high risk, 28 as moderate risk and 18 as general risk areas. Following the survey findings, the city corporation has already launched special mosquito control drives in high-risk areas. DSCC authorities said dengue cannot be completely eliminated through government or city corporation initiatives alone. Residents must keep their homes and workplaces clean and develop the habit of removing stagnant clean water at least once a week. The corporation also expects strong public cooperation and an active role from the media in building a dengue free and livable city. Meanwhile, DSCC Administrator Md Abdus Salam said mosquito control activities were being intensified by identifying high risk areas. “According to the survey findings, mosquito control activities are being intensified. However, dengue cannot be controlled by spraying insecticides alone. Public awareness is essential,” he said. PHOTO BY NICOLE DROEGER Facebook Twitter WhatsApp SMS Email Print Copy article link Save A mosquito buzzing in your backyard may seem like a minor annoyance. But these tiny insects, with their taste for human blood, are increasingly appearing in areas where they were once rare or absent, and that’s raising concerns about the spread of mosquito-borne diseases, including West Nile, Zika and dengue fever. Florida’s struggles with dengue fever in 2026 should be a warning. Hillsborough County, home to Tampa, had seen more than 350 dengue cases, at least one of them fatal, by late October. Miami-Dade County had reported more than 200 cases, and the statewide number was still rising in what has been described as the largest dengue outbreak in modern Florida history. There has also been a case in Sarasota County with a woman who was hospitalized, during which time she was extremely sick and lost 17 pounds. More than 400 of the over 700 Florida cases, including many of those in Hillsborough County and at least seven in the Orlando area, were listed as locally acquired from mosquitoes in the area. Climate change is part of the reason people in many parts of the country are seeing more mosquitoes. Rising global temperatures and shorter winters expand the area suitable for mosquitoes to live in and transmit viruses that cause diseases. Climate change also brings increasingly erratic storm systems, heat and rainfall patterns that leave standing water, creating conditions ideal for mosquitoes to breed. The other major factor shaping where mosquitoes live, often overlooked, is humans themselves. We study entomology and medical geography, including the spread of mosquito-borne diseases. To understand why you may be seeing more mosquitoes, and why communities like Hillsborough County are spending millions of dollars on attempts to control them, start by looking close to home. MOSQUITOS FOLLOW HUMANS Mosquitoes such as Aedes aegypti — the primary transmitter of pathogens that cause dengue fever, yellow fever, Chikungunya and Zika in the Americas — likely arrived in the U.S. with the slave trade. Both Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus, a transmitter of many of the same diseases but a more recent arrival in the U.S., are moved by the global shipping network, which can take them to new locations and reintroduce them in parts of their ranges where they may have been controlled in the past. Aedes aegypti’s habits, including its ability to use household environments for living and breeding, have made it a very successful and established invader where climate conditions permit. A flowerpot saucer, clogged gutter, discarded tire, birdbath or even a bottle cap can collect enough water for mosquito larvae to develop. A single Aedes aegypti mosquito can lay more than 100 eggs at a time up to five times during its lifespan, which is only about a month. As suburban neighborhoods expand, so do opportunities for mosquitoes to breed and find humans for their meals. Across the United States, new housing developments create thousands of these small water-holding containers and bring together the two things these mosquitoes need: standing water and people. This combination allows them to spread through transportation networks, establishing populations far from their original ranges, and explains why mosquito expansion is often linked to patterns of human movement and development. Aedes albopictus, originally native to Southeast Asia and now found in all habitable continents, provides a striking example of this spread. These mosquitoes arrived in the U.S. mostly because of human actions. They stowed away on boats and other vehicles, often riding in used tires or lucky bamboo. Their early dispersal in the U.S. has been linked to the interstate highway system. By 2017, Aedes albopictus was documented in 1,368 counties across 40 states, and it has continued to expand across much of the eastern and central U.S. One of Iowa’s first established Aedes albopictus populations, for example, appeared in the Des Moines metropolitan area, where it has continued to grow and expand to other communities. Its spread from Southeast Asia all the way to the U.S. Midwest demonstrates how globalization and suburban growth can create opportunities for mosquitoes. MOST COMMON THREAT: WEST NILE West Nile virus remains the most widespread mosquito-borne disease in the continental United States. It is primarily transmitted by Culex mosquitoes, including common house mosquitoes, which are found in much of the country. Culex mosquitoes can breed in a wide range of habitats, including storm drains, roadside ditches, retention ponds, wetlands and other standing water. Their ability to thrive in both urban and rural environments has helped make West Nile virus an enduring public health concern in many states. Because Culex mosquitoes are already established across much of the country, climate change may not necessarily introduce them to new regions. Instead, research is increasingly focused on how changing temperatures and precipitation patterns could influence their abundance, seasonal activity and ability to transmit disease. Researchers found that New York state’s season with temperatures suitable for mosquitoes to transmit West Nile virus lengthened by an average of 20 days between 1999 and 2024. A study conducted by one of us, Sadie Ryan, showed that in Florida, all 67 counties had a suitable season for mosquitoes spreading West Nile virus for five or more months in 2000, and 2.33 million people in Florida experienced a nine-month-long season. Just recently, Sarasota County confirmed had a recent case of West Nile. By the 2030s, as temperatures warm, the study projects that around 70% of Florida’s population is likely to have a chance of getting West Nile nine months out of the year. In 2025, for example, Florida took longer to cool down in the fall than usual, leaving moderate temperatures and enough standing water that Aedes mosquitoes could remain active late into the year. Florida saw a rise in dengue cases. Longer warm seasons means mosquitoes will become a growing public health issue, and controlling them will become increasingly crucial. Listen to this article 3 min Florida health officials have confirmed 485 locally acquired cases of dengue fever this year, as the state grapples with its largest outbreak in decades. Between Oct. 18 and Oct. 24, state surveillance logged 60 new infections, with the Tampa Bay area accounting for roughly 95% of all locally acquired cases recorded statewide, according to the Florida Department of Health. The surge prompted emergency declarations in Hillsborough, Pasco and Pinellas counties in late September, allowing for faster purchasing and spraying and requests for state and federal reimbursement. Hillsborough County has since extended its state of local emergency amid ongoing transmission. DENGUE FEVER OUTBREAK TRIGGERS STATES OF EMERGENCY IN 3 SOUTHERN COUNTIES The locally acquired infections are separate from more than 300 travel-associated dengue cases reported in Florida this year. The Florida Mosquito Control Association said mosquito abatement teams are stepping up targeted ground spraying, aerial applications and localized property inspections. Mosquito-control crews across the Tampa Bay area have increased surveillance and treatments as locally acquired dengue cases climb. (iStock) What is dengue fever? Dengue is a viral illness transmitted primarily through the bite of infected Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus mosquitoes. The virus can cause fever, severe muscle and joint pain, nausea, rash and, in severe cases, dangerous complications or death, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Unlike many mosquito species that bite mostly at dawn and dusk, the mosquitoes carrying dengue feed aggressively during daytime hours and thrive in humid residential environments. In addition to local spread, Florida has tracked more than 300 travel-associated infections this year, which continue to introduce the virus to domestic mosquito populations. supplementary_news.content: Another health outbreak is on the loose. This time, Florida is the state most heavily impacted. Videos by Wide Open Country According to a Monday (November 2) report from Fox News Digital, Florida Health Officials have confirmed 485 "locally acquired" cases of Dengue Fever in the Sunshine State. They have defined the outbreak as the largest in years (via The New York Post). Several Cases of Dengue Fever Reported in Florida Per the report, Florida health officials logged 60 new cases of the virus between October 18 and October 24. The largest number of new cases came from Tampa Bay. The city accounted for more than 90% of the new cases. Additionally, more than 300 "travel-associated" cases of Dengue Fever were reported in the state earlier in 2026. Following the release of the report, there was a bevy of reactions on social media. "And just like that, they have their excuse lined up for more genetically engineered mosquitoes to be dropped in Florida," one user wrote on X, formerly known as Twitter. "Funny how [Dengue] spread exactly where they released the genetically modified mosquitoes to stop dengue, but it's just a conspiracy theory, not a coincidence," a second user chimed in. "I don't trust anything dealing with this government," a third user remarked. New Virus Derives From Mosquitoes Dengue fever is an illness from mosquito bites that happens in tropical and subtropical areas of the world (via Mayo Clinic). The Aedes mosquito is the most recognizable carrier of the virus. It can cause a high fever and flu-like symptoms. "The Aedes mosquitoes that can transmit dengue are active during the day and thrive in warm, humid environments like those found in Florida," an entomologist spokesperson at the SC Johnson Center for Insect Science and Family Health told Fox News Digital. The spokesperson also added: "Staying aware of local mosquito activity and consistently protecting against bites are important steps people can take to help reduce their risk." Other symptoms can include - Headache. - Muscle, bone, or joint pain. - Upset stomach. - Vomiting. - Pain behind the eyes. - Swollen glands. - Rash. A more serious form of dengue fever, called dengue hemorrhagic fever, can cause bleeding, a sudden drop in blood pressure, and death. Symptoms of the more serious form of dengue fever include: - Bad stomach pain. - Repeated vomiting. - Bleeding from the gums or nose. - Blood in the urine, stools, or vomit. - Bleeding under the skin, which might look like bruising. - Hard or fast breathing. - Tiredness. - Being cranky or restless. Those experiencing those symptoms should immediately seek medical attention

supplementary_news.title: 海南三亚工地爆登革热疫情 数千工人被隔离
supplementary_news.excerpt: 海南省三亚市多个高端住宅工地近日爆发登革热疫情,数千名建筑工人随后被封控隔离,多名工人向大纪元透露,工地疑已有数十至数百人感染,全员被多次抽血检测。部分工人被转移至当地酒店或居民小区,引发事前不知情的小区业主不满。时值中共二十届五中全会在北京召开,敏感的时间节点使防控全面升级。据悉,三亚市市长亲赴现场督导,警方24小时严密把守入口,严禁人员随意进出,防控措施极为严苛。
